speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would not want to let the twenty fifth anniversary of the national film board, a corporation which Canada should rightly be proud of, go by without mentioning that fact to the house.
It was on May 2, 1939, that the royal assent was given to the bill establishing the national film board. If we look up the record, we see that the members unanimously recognized the necessity of creating an agency whose function would be to produce and distribute films in the national interest.
The act clearly defined the role of the
board: to produce, among other things, appropriate films which would get Canadians to know one another better and make everybody more deeply aware of the scope and diversity of their country. In the National Film Act, as revised in 1950, one of the tasks of the national film board was defined along the same lines but in a broader sense. The new act provided that the board should produce and distribute and also promote the production and distribution of films designed to interpret Canada to Canadians and to other nations.

Mr. Speaker, it is not my intention to dwell at great length on how well the national film board has achieved those stated objectives. I believe this has been amply proven in the past 25 years. Moreover, recognition has been won throughout the world in open competition against the best films that other countries could produce. National film board productions are being shown to groups in communities here and abroad as well as on theatre screens and on television in Canada and in more than 100 other countries. Every day brings further evidence of the value and influence of national film board productions as a positive force for telling Canada's story effectively.
On this twenty fifth anniversary of its formation I should like to extend sincere congratulations to the national film board, its management and its personnel for the effective results achieved in its first 25 years, together with the wish that the future may enhance the board's usefulness to Canada and add further laurels to the many it has already won.

It has trained technicians, specialists and qualified people in the field of film industry.
But even if we celebrate today the twenty fifth anniversary of the national film board, this should not be a time to rest on our laurels, especially when there is a very pronounced trend in Canada toward the setting

subtopic: STATEMENT WITH RESPECT TO STOCKPILING PROGRAM
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, in the absence of the Minister of Trade and Commerce I should like to make the following statement regarding uranium stockpiling. The

government has reviewed the uranium situation in the light of the latest available information and has come to the conclusion that it would not be advisable to extend the stockpiling policy beyond the one year period specified in the Prime Minister's announcement of June 26, 1963.
By the end of this period the government will have invested about $25 million in a uranium stockpile. This policy was designed to provide a breathing space for the affected communities by enabling certain mines to maintain employment until July 1, 1964.
While the present stockpile will be useful in ensuring continuity of supplies, it is the government's view that continued stockpiling would have a depressing effect on the markets for uranium. It would hold back the revival of demand for which, as the Prime Minister said in his June, 1963 statement, the eventual prospects are good. In the meantime the government is continuing to explore the development of alternative sources of employment in the communities where there are uranium mines.

Answer: The department's attention was drawn to allegedly large catches of eulachon by herring seiners. The allegation was to the effect that eulachon were being taken in quantities from a few pounds to thousands of tons.
The facts are that on March 8 because of poor fishing three herring seiners moved into Iceberg bay in the Nass estuary to prospect. This was not normal in that sets for herring are not usually made above Somerville island. One seiner made a set and found eulachon rather than herring. He immediately spilled the net. However, some eulachon did hang up in his net and they were sold with the herring he had.
It is felt that the circumstances were unusual and that present protection for eulachon will be ample.

Answer: 1 and 2. Order in council P.C. 535 January 27, 1944 states in part as follows:
"Eldorado Mining and Refining Limited is hereby declared to be a body corporate and politic within the legislative authority of the parliament of Canada, but, on the issue of letters patent by the Secretary of State, as hereinafter provided, shall be a body corporate and politic without share capital, and shall consist of such persons as are from time to time named by the minister of munitions and supply, and shall have for its purpose the exercise and performance in Canada or elsewhere, without pecuniary gain to such corporation, of such of the powers and duties conferred or imposed on the minister of munitions and supply as the minister of munitions and supply desired to delegate to such corporation."

speechtext:
The next major step forward in this program was the statement made in February, 1958 in the city of Winnipeg by the then prime minister of Canada, now Leader of the Opposition. That was the occasion when in specific detail the national development program of the government of that time was put forward. The city of Winnipeg was chosen for a very good reason. It is right in the centre of Canada geographically. It has always been regarded as the gateway to the west and the north, and it would seem to be the pivotal point around which any major, massive, national development program should take place.
I want to pick out one specific point that was raised on that occasion. At that meeting the prime minister of that time called for the convening of a conference on conservation, on the wise management and multiple use of Canada's renewable resources. The challenge issued was a challenge to all the people of Canada. AH levels of government and industry as well as the educational leaders of the nation were challenged to come together in a conference that would be convened by the federal government in order to deal with the critical situation in Canada's natural resources.
The crisis was all the more urgent and deepseated because of the long years of neglect to which I have already referred. To show how quickly the challenge was met, I point out that the first meeting to bring about a conference of this kind took place on November 17, 1958, I believe, and the response to the challenge as demonstrated at that meeting was overwhelmingly positive. It was a clear indication that all levels of government, particularly the provincial governments, were aware of the situation that had been outlined by the prime minister. A steering committee was formed which was made up of representatives of each of the provincial governments, and plans proceeded rapidly to bring about a gathering of Canadians from all walks of life in order to meet the challenge of the crisis that had been created by long years of neglect.
Perhaps it would be useful to outline why the situation had been allowed to deteriorate to the serious level which made such dramatic action necessary. It was only in the early part of this century that Canadians began to realize that our resources were not unlimited. We had been largely motivated by the frontier concept of there always being new worlds to conquer; therefore we had proceeded to waste our rich heritage of natural resources, particularly our renewal resources.


The first attempt to which I have referred briefly, occured in the early part of the century, but it was a conservationist approach in the negative sense. The problem was approached from the static concept which conceived of saving or preserving resources rather than making the best economic use of them. The challenge that was issued by the prime minister in 1958 involved a new, positive concept of wise management and the planning of the development of our resources in that it was geared to the economic needs of the nation. Instead of being a static, preservationist concept, it viewed the development of these resources in terms of the economy into which Canada was moving in the post-war world.
The basic problem, of course, in meeting a challenge of this kind is that of overcoming the areas of jurisdictional dispute. The resources belong to the provinces. The initiative to develop national policies belongs to the federal government. I think this is the major reason why for years there had been such serious neglect. The old buck passing or log rolling technique had been used with a vengeance by both the federal and provincial levels of government. If a problem was brought before the house it was ignored simply by making the statement that this was a matter that came under provincial jurisdiction. In order to get anywhere with a national development program the buck passing technique had to be overcome. The fundamental approach, therefore, of the planning for what became known as the resources for tomorrow conference was to deal with this area of dispute as between provincial responsibility and federal responsibility.
The warm, positive response of the steering committee was manifest from the outset and was a demonstration of the success that was going to crown the efforts of this important federal initiative. More important even than the steering committee, made up of provincial ministers, were the advisory committees that were organized to develop and support the efforts of the steering committee. There was brought together for the first time a group of Canadians who represented a broad body of knowledge in the field of renewable resources. This was the first time any attempt had been made to bring together Canadian human resources capable of meeting the challenge of this problem.
During the period of preparation, which occupied some two years, there was brought together a group of experts on soil, water, wildlife, forest conservation, and so on. Background papers were prepared numbering more than 80 I think, important as the conference itself was, this great body of experts and body of information that was brought together in

order to make that resources for tomorrow conference the great success that it was, when it finally took place in 1961, was even more important. I believe too that it was the first successful model for the type of co-operative federalism that has been mentioned in recent months. This discussion and preparing of plans for our renewable resources was described as an exercise in co-operative federalism. It was quite a different exercise from those that have taken place in recent months. This was consultation in anticipation and not retroactivity. In other words the federal government, realizing it was making initiatives in a very sensitive area of federal-provincial jurisdictional dispute, consulted with the provincial leaders. As a result there was complete harmony when the conference took place which ushered in the positive results with which I shall deal in a moment.
Unfortunately this term "co-operative federalism" has been bandied around to such an extent that it describes all sorts of encounters between the provinces and the federal government. It is almost in as much disrepute semantically as the word "peace" used to be in the days when those who were not necessarily in pursuit of peace used to refer to themselves as "the peace loving peoples of the world". If you are going to get co-operation in dealings with the provinces, I submit to the government you cannot get co-operation after the event. We have had enough experience with the problems that have been created by the failure to consult, by the failure to give recognition to the area of authority of the provincial government in recent months. You must consult in anticipation rather than following frustration in dealing with these problems.
As a result, even before the conference itself was held various positive results began to be seen, and this in the face of changes of government at the provincial level while these preparations were going on, changes of ministers at the federal level and at the provincial level. For example, the so-called quiet revolution in Quebec took place during the period of preparation for the conference, and it was thought that there would be difficulty with the new administration in Quebec. The minister who joined the steering committee representing Quebec was Hon. Rene Levesque, who was the holder of certain viewpoints concerning matters pertaining to federal-provincial co-operation. Mr. Levesque joined the steering committee, and it is interesting to note he became one of the most enthusiastic supporters for the idea of the resources for tomorrow conference, an excellent illustration of how a reasonable and responsible approach to these matters can achieve re-
Canadian. Water Resources suits. When it was decided to proceed with the program it was decided that the resources ministers council, backed by a secretariat, would be located in the city of Montreal. Incidentally, it was to be a completely bilingual secretariat. This action represented a new concept in overcoming this jurisdictional problem in that it was a secretariat responsible to Ottawa and responsible to the provinces, and also at the service of the universities, and private industry. Canadians interested in the resources field felt that this was a major break-through in real co-operative federalism.

The establishment of the resource ministers council took place in September, 1962, I believe, and the meeting was held in the city of Toronto.
In order to demonstrate the sincerity of the intent and purpose of the federal government, to indicate that we were following what could best be described as a basis of co-equality between the levels of government-because when you are in the sensitive area of resource development it has to be approached on the basis of co-equality-the device of a rotating chairmanship was created. The chairman of the steering committee was the federal minister. He was also chairman of the conference, and the first chairman of the resource ministers council. The chairmanship then passed on to the representative of the province of Ontario. The next chairman was the representative of the province of Quebec, and it was during the period of his chairmanship that the character of this program that could genuinely be called co-operative faderalism was initiated. The current chairman is the minister of resources for Prince Edward Island, and the fact that this is the centennial year for Prince Edward Island was one reason the torch was passed to that minister during this very important period in the history of that province.
Here is a successful and genuine effort at overcoming one of the major problems of national development by an exercise in co-operative federalism in anticipation instead of by hindsight.

Yes, after frustration. As I was pointing out, this enthusiasm, contrasted with the frustration in programs of mutual responsibility today, was such that the governments agreed to proceed with the major program of resource development before the conference had even met. I refer to the ARDA program, the Agricultural Rehabilitation and Development Act passed by this house in the

Canadian Water Resources spring of 1961. The conference did not take place until the fall of 1961. Here is a major breakthrough in rural redevelopment, in the wise management and the multiple use of our renewable resources. If it is applied with the initiative that is necessary at the federal level it could go a long way in dealing with the problem I am specifically going to bring before the house this afternoon.
The national wildlife federation emerged out of the resources for tomorrow conference. It is the first attempt in this country to bring together, on a national basis, the problems of conservation in the important area of wildlife. The federal-provincial parks conference was another by-product of the resources for tomorrow conference, but unfortunately it has been dormant in recent months, again because the initiative must come from the federal government level.
In the interest of recreational development and the wise management of all our renewable resources, the national parks association got under way early last year. This was a spontaneous response by the people of Canada to the conference. It is not connected with any government. It is the coming together of people interested in the wise management of resources. One of the leading figures in the movement is Mr. William Baker, who had been the co-ordinator for recreational and parks matters in planning for the resources for tomorrow conference.
As could be anticipated, Mr. Speaker, there was participation in that conference at the top level. The Governor General launched the conference. The prime minister of Canada made a major statement, as did the premier of Quebec and other leaders representing the other parts of Canada. The prime minister's statement was most significant because he was the leader charged with the responsibility of continuing the momentum that had been established by this very excellent conference.
Realizing that he was dealing in the sensitive area of resource development he prefaced his proposals with the words "with the consent and co-operation of the provincial governments," but we in the federal government had to bring something to a head. We had to take advantage of the good will that was generated by this important conference. I shall mention three of the proposals which the then prime minister made. His first was that there should be regular conferences of this type in order to continue the momentum. That was pointed out three years ago, but unfortunately in the interim there has been a slowing down of the momentum.
Second, he proposed the resource ministers council which has now become a reality, and is operating most successfully in the city of Montreal. Third, he urged the establishment of

a national advisory land and water use board, and he specifically emphasized the urgency of the matter in respect to water resources because already the crisis was upon us. Unfortunately, up to the present time nothing has been done in this area. There has been a whole slowing down of the process of coequality, intergovernmental co-operation, and the initiative represented by ARDA, the federal-provincial parks conference, and the other matters to which I have referred, all because there has been a lack of leadership at the federal government level.
Indeed, there has been so much dispute, controversy and misunderstanding during recent months that one could hardly anticipate it would have been possible. I have reviewed the history because unless we reviewed the sudden change in the co-operative climate of Canada which has taken place since April, 1963, it would be impossible to appreciate the enormity of that change. In the resource area we moved together with absolute understanding and co-operation, and I may say this is the most sensitive area of federal-provincial jurisdictional dispute. Unfortunately the whole picture has been blurred and disrupted just at the time when the conservation crises was becoming most severe.
Why did the right hon. Leader of the Opposition suggest and urge that a national advisory board be established on water conservation? The answer is abundantly clear. It became abundantly clear during the preparation of the resources for tomorrow conference that we had reached a point of no return in the wise management of this basic resource. Water is basic to the well being of the nation. It is basic to all human life. Though the North American continent, and Canada in particular, seemingly has an abundance of fresh water resources, Canada, with its relatively small population as compared with other industrialized nations of the world, is already faced with critical problems in the water resource area.
Right here on our doorstep we have water pollution in the Ottawa river. This is one river which has been badly polluted in recent years. We have a water shortage in the great lakes. There is a critical water shortage problem throughout southern Ontario. It is a problem that covers the whole area of the Canadian economy as well as all aspects of life. Whether you fish in it, whether you sail boats on it-this is the recreational aspect- whether you put it on crops or whether you build summer cottages beside it, water is; vital and fundamental to the continuing progress and prosperity of the Canadian economy.
It is the one vital renewable resource and, if it is to be wisely managed for the future, it must have applied to it the multiple use

concept that was put forward in that speech in Winnipeg in 1958. Why have we neglected it thus far? The remarks I made with reference to our general attitude to renewable resources apply here. There is the seeming abundance of it.
The British North America Act was a very wise document but it failed to recognize the interrelationships that exist among all our renewable resources, and up until recent times the only federal initiative in the area of water resources was the interest of the Canadian government in navigation and fishery matters. It was the provinces who led in attacking the problem. They were forced to because there was no response from the federal government. The province of Ontario, under a Conservative government-and it is more than coincidence that Conservative governments have always been identified with positive approaches to conservation matters- established the water resources commission in order to deal with the problem in Ontario. But a province by itself cannot deal with it. The hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam will be fully aware that it is beyond the capacity of an individual province to deal with.
In bringing this matter before the house this afternoon I do not have to go into details. We have the documentation of the resources for tomorrow conference, three volumes of which spell out in detail the message that the crisis is upon us. It was for this reason that the prime minister of the previous Conservative government put his finger on this one aspect as the most urgent and critical problem. It was for this reason that the previous Conservative administration introduced the sewage disposal plan which has been so eminently successful, at least in one area, that of dealing with the problem of pollution which had reached such a crisis that the major cities of Canada were short of adequate, fresh water supplies. It was for this reason that we used the Canada Water Conservation Act, which had been on the statute books of Canada since the early 1950's but had never been used, to support such major watershed control programs as the metro Toronto water conservation program where, for the first time in Canadian history a comprehensive and massive approach is being made to resolving the water problems of that city. It was for this reason that the government proceeded with the construction of the Saskatchewan dam, which project had been criticized by the previous Liberal administration, with the exception of the minister of agriculture Hon. James Gardiner, who was one of the first to congratulate the government of Right Hon. John Diefenbaker when it made the decision to go ahead with
Canadian Water Resources this vital, multiple-use water control program on the prairies. It was for this reason, too, that the water control program on the Saint John river was proceeded with.
These all went forward in the comparatively short period that the Conservative government was in office, and the initiative was indicated by that important statement that was made in 1958. I would suggest to the government, Mr. Speaker, that there has been a slow down; there has been a tragic loss of momentum. The problems were urgent and critical a year ago; they are more so now, because there has been no new initiative of any kind in this area, notwithstanding the promise of the present government of 60 days of decision that would shake the nation. There has been no new initiative in this area of renewable resource development. Therefore, Mr. Speaker-and others will be specific concerning ARDA and other problems that I have merely outlined to the house in preparation of the amendment-I move, seconded by the hon. member for Victoria-Carleton (Mr. Flemming):
That the motion be amended by striking out all the words after "that" and substituting therefor:
This house condemns the neglect of the government in failing to establish a co-ordinated national water policy and in ignoring the imminent national crisis in water resources management, which is evidenced by the critical low water levels of the great lakes and other national waters, the increasing pollution of national waters-
Perhaps we could-just by way of aside -have included in that "the increasing pollution of the political life of the nation", but that is not in the amendment here. It says- and I repeat the last few words-
-the increasing pollution of national waters, and the urgent necessity of conserving water resources for the benefit of national resource development in Canada;
And urges the government, in the interests of national development, to take immediate action to make up for their year of neglect of this problem by forthwith:
(1)	establishing a national advisory committee on water resources to assist in co-ordinating national resource development;
(2)	accelerating the application of ARDA policies to the problems of national resource development, and,
(3)	vigorously continuing and expanding the water and other resource development programs conceived and established by the previous Conservative government.

Mr. Speaker, I had intended to wait my turn until later, but if no other hon. member at this moment is prepared to speak on this very important subject, I would like to speak on it myself, with particular reference to water levels. I would particularly mention the very serious problem facing this country in connection with water levels on the great lakes and the St. Lawrence seaway system. There

Canadian Water Resources are actually two grounds of complaint that I wish to put forward in supporting this motion, which sets out the very clear and consistent policy of resource development that was initiated by the previous government, and the fact that no continuation of this policy is in evidence.
I want particularly to mention first the failure of the present government to recognize the dangers of the situation which has developed since last summer with regard to low water levels; and second, the complete breakdown as far as we can see of any co-ordination of effort on the part of the government. These are the two particular subjects with which I wish to deal. As far as the first is concerned, the failure to recognize the dangers of the situation, despite persistent questioning by members of the official opposition over the past several weeks, there is no evidence of any real concern on the part of the government in regard to this serious problem. When any individual member of the government is pressed into a corner by persistent questioning, we get the general answer which is, in effect, "There is nothing we can do". We have pressed our questioning on various members of the government in an effort to find out whether they really understand that there is a serious situation and that something can be done about it.
Despite many useful suggestions with regard to courses of action that can be taken, we have had no indication from the government that any such action is contemplated or is under consideration. It may be said that there is not anything that can be done, that this is an act of God and is caused by a lack of precipitation, and that we just have to pray for rain, as the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) once stated. There are many people in this country, and I am one of them, who believe that there is something that can be done. There is something that can be done on a short term basis, and there is something that can be done on a long term basis.
For example, last week we had indications in the press that there were major works being contemplated at the exit from lake Huron by the United States corps of engineers. They are proposing to construct certain concrete weirs or, as they were described today in answer to a question from the hon. member for Simcoe East (Mr. Rynard), submerged sills, which will have the effect of slowing down the outrush of waters from lake Huron which ultimately find their way out of the St. Lawrence river and into the sea. We did have an indication that this was being done. Last week another hon. member and myself raised this matter and the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) answered it in
IMr. Aiken.]

general terms. He said that there was a water problem but made no reference whatever to the question of co-operating with the United States corps of engineers.
We believe, Mr. Speaker, that an inquiry should be undertaken into the amount of water being taken out of the great lakes at Chicago and elsewhere. This question has been raised year after year and we are still in doubt as to whether or not the amount of water being removed from the great lakes system at Chicago is that which is contemplated by the international agreement. Many people believe that there is more water being taken out than is realized. There is before the house at the present time a notice of motion in the name of the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue (Mr. Martineau) concerning the grand canal concept, which is a diversion of waters from the Harricanaw and other rivers flowing into James bay to be taken into the great lakes system. It is interesting to note that the United States authorities have indicated that this seems to be the only answer they can devise to offer any long term solution. We have not heard anything from this government as to whether or not they are going to undertake feasibility studies on this project. Since this is the only answer which has been forthcoming on the long term, surely the government is giving some thought to the question; and I am sure that the hon. member for Pontiac-Temiscamingue will be raising the matter again at the very first opportunity. It is something which can be done, even if it is a long term project. Feasibility studies on this project would undoubtedly prove successful and we hope that the project can be undertaken.
Another project which can be undertaken, Mr. Speaker, concerns temporary access to wharves on the great lakes and on Georgian bay. I am glad to see the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Deschatelets) in the house because he made a statement on Friday during the course of his estimates with regard to dredging. I agree that as far as he went there is ground for caution in connection with dredging along the edges of wharves which are now troubled by low water conditions. I am sure that this is something which has to be dealt with carefully. But there is an aspect about which I questioned him the previous day and which he did not deal with, and I should like to draw it to his attention now. This is the question of access to wharves where there is sufficient water but where the wharf is now five or six feet above the surface of the water. For example, in my riding two or three major wharves on Georgian bay have plenty of water for boats to get in, but there is no way of reaching the

surface of the wharf from a small boat, or even from a medium sized boat. Temporary-emergency measures are required in order to provide steps or a temporary platform, or something by means of which people can reach the top of the wharf. I am sure there are many wharves in this position.
I have been told that on one of the wharves on Georgian bay at Pointe au Baril people have to beach their boats some distance away from the wharf and walk around to it. A week last Saturday night a man fell off the wharf while trying to get onto it from his boat, because the top of the wharf was too high above the level of the water. Emergency measures should also be undertaken to construct walkways where there is insufficient water to use the wharf. I think these matters must be considered, and in addition dredging is feasible in some places. Here are four or five definite projects which could be started on immediately, one of them long range, others short range and immediate, to reach the waters and to keep navigation going.
This is not just a local problem on the great lakes and Georgian bay; it is a national problem. Its first and major effect is on shipping, and not just on the small boats but also on the larger vessels. It affects the carriage of grain, which in turn affects all of Canada. There is difficulty in getting into some of the elevators. There is a difficulty in connection with elevator facilities. I am told by the hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Noble) that some of the grain boats are finding difficulty in getting into the Owen Sound elevators. I am also told by the hon. member for Simcoe East, who is listening, that there are problems involving delays to shipbuilding at Collingwood. These problems which I have mentioned concern more than just small boat navigation; they are major problems.
Then there is another point relating to small boats, which is directly a tourist problem; and unless some action is taken immediately or some long term project is promised, I am sure there is going to be a serious discouragement to tourists and a decline in the use of tourist facilities. It is going to be very serious this summer. People are prepared sometimes to put up with minor inconveniences if they expect to put up with them for just one season, and that the following year there will be improvement; but unfortunately the forecast I have seen is that there may be, and most likely will be, a water shortage again next year.
I believe it is essential that the government give some indication that they are doing something about this problem and can give us some hope that late in 1964 or in 1965 this work will be done. Many people believe that a quick answer is available with regard 20220-183
Canadian Water Resources to the slowing down of the outflow of water from lake Huron, but we have had no indication of this. If the tourist business suffers this year it will result in one of Canada's major sources of foreign currency being badly cut down. Since about 1961 there has been a constant increase in our currency exchange with the United States, owing to tourist revenues. Prior to 1961 the situation was bad in that regard, but it has gradually improved, and if this improvement is now damaged by the discouragement of tourists we will have not only a local problem on the great lakes and in Georgian bay but a currency problem for all Canada.
We also have loss of water resources. If it is true that there is an unusual outflow of water from lake Huron and that it is escaping more than ever into the St. Lawrence river and thence into the sea, we are losing all of those benefits which come with water. I have tried to outline only some of the serious dangers we are facing in Canada in this regard. I hope the government is undertaking measures which will relieve the fears of so many people, but so far we have had nothing except evasion, and evasive answers to questions.
The purpose of this motion and of my complaint is not to place the blame for the low water on anyone. It is a situation which we have to face. My hon. friend from Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) indicated that a water resource policy had been embarked upon, but that it seems to be slipping. Regardless of what has happened in the past, it is obvious from the figures that the levels of water in the great lakes are seriously low. I do not blame the government for this in the short term. I am trying to show-and I hope to be able to prove this before I am finished-that low precipitation is not the sole cause. This is where blame attaches to the government; they have accepted too easily this plausible explanation-lack of rain. Certain figures were given to us today in answer to question 661. It is true that precipitation has been lower, but the shortage of rain does not seem sufficiently serious to explain the results in terms of the significant lowering of water levels. There must be other causes. I have suggested some of them, and I think the government would do well to recognize that the present situation is a result of causes other than lack of precipitation. If the government really believes that this is just a matter of insufficient rain, and that we shall have to wait until more rain falls, then I think the administration deserves the condemnation of the house.
I blame the government for not having taken action when the problem became apparent. I blame them for not making a full

Canadian Water Resources inquiry into the situation. I blame them for not having taken action to meet the immediate difficulties and I blame them for failing to indicate long term plans designed to prevent a similar situation in the future. The government's attitude, I believe, was succinctly summed up by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) when he told us to pray for rain. I would remind the hon. gentleman of another saying: "The Lord helps those who help themselves" and I think we shall have to do something in this case to help ourselves, not merely sit back and wait for rain. Lack of precipitation has simply been used as an excuse for not taking action. Certainly, precipitation was lower in 1963 than it was in 1962 and previous years. But it was not lower by very much. In answer to question 655, it was stated that precipitation for 1961 in the upper great lakes area amounted to 28.58 inches. For 1962, it was 27.19 inches, and for 1963, 25.30 inches. There has been a decrease of about three inches in total precipitation in those three years. But in 1956 precipitation amounted only to 27.01 inches, and this is not abnormal.
We were given an answer today to question 661 in relation to a slightly different area. We find that in 1961, precipitation amounted to 30.52. In 1962, it was 28.62 and in 1963 it was 27.32. It is true there was a slightly smaller amount of precipitation in the latter year but the decline is not related to the great difference of between three and five feet in lake levels over the same period of time. The one situation cannot be the sole cause of the other.
This brings me to the question of lake levels. In 1962, according to the answer to a question asked recently, the United States corps of engineers deepened the channel between lake Huron and lake St. Clair by some six feet. It has been stated on several occasions that since the water levels of lake Huron and lake St. Clair are approximately the same it would not really matter whether they deepened the channel by 20 feet-the outflow would be no different. But in question 655 I inquired as to the lake levels of lake Huron, lake St. Clair and lake Erie. The answer is a direct indication of the flow of water. The figures began in 1955. According to the international great lakes datum the level of lake Huron was 579.01 feet. Lake St. Clair was 574.11 and lake Erie, 571.49. In other words, lake St. Clair was five feet lower than lake Huron and lake Erie was two and a half feet lower than lake St. Clair.
In 1963 we find the level of lake Huron was 576.51 feet; lake St. Clair was 571.78 feet and lake Erie was 569.44 feet. These figures indicate that there is definitely a very


considerable difference between these lake levels, and therefore that any outflow of waters would be seriously increased by the deepening of the channels. We also find that between 1962 and 1963 the level of lake Huron went down by one foot, and lake Erie only by six inches-these are average levels. This indicates an uneveness in the outflow of water from lake Huron. These figures belie the casual statement that there is no difference in the outflow of waters caused by channel construction. It is obvious that there is a difference, and it is a serious difference.
We also notice that the level of the St. Lawrence at Montreal has not declined to the extent of the upper waters; while it is lower, the difference is not serious. So we are faced with a situation where water is being drawn out from the upper lakes and allowed to flow through the St. Lawrence seaway to the ocean. We would like to know whether more water is escaping from the upper lakes than ought to be escaping.
I mentioned the United States corps of engineers. Very recently we found they were experimenting with weirs or sills to see if they could slow down the outflow of water from lake Huron. I believe the very fact they have been undertaking these experiments indicates their belief that there is another factor besides precipitation involved and, in the second place, that there is something which can be done about it. The Canadian government has certainly given no indication that it is any more than casually interested in these experiments.
Last week I gave the Minister of Transport (Mr. Pickersgill) the opportunity to state that his department was involved in these experiments. Both the hon. member for Lambton West (Mr. Foy) and myself raised the same question on the same day and became involved in a sort of competition to see which of us could get the right to make use of the adjournment debate procedure. In fact we both were successful in getting the right to speak in the adjournment debate on the subject of the experiments being undertaken. The Minister of Transport spoke for three minutes in answer to the question of the hon. member for Lambton West and for three minutes in answer to my question and he never mentioned the experiments at all. We wonder how much co-operation there is and how interested the government is in seeking a solution to the problem.
Another indication is the levels of the inland lakes. If the problem was purely a lack of precipitation one would expect to find that the water levels in most of the inland lakes would be low. This is not the case. The water level of lake Nipissing, which empties into the Georgian bay through the French river,

on April 23, 1964 was one foot higher than it was last year and approximately the same amount over the level in 1962. This surely does not indicate that there is a shortage of water. Certainly lake Nipissing has a control dam by which, under an agreement, the level is kept as close as possible to where it should be, but if the water was just not there the level certainly could not be maintained no matter how many dams were installed.
The same thing applies to the Muskoka lakes. I reside in that area and I am very well acquainted with them. The Muskoka lakes are normal-a little bit down, a matter of inches, but in effect their levels are normal. In most of the other inland lakes in Ontario about which I have inquired the levels are normal, and if the problem were a straight case of no precipitation then surely the levels of these lakes would be down as well. These are the things that make us wonder whether the very simple answer, lack of precipitation, is in fact the whole answer. I think there is something more involved.
After expounding on what I believe to be the lack of action on the part of the government and an improper assessment of the real situation, I should like to go on to my second point. It concerns the lack of co-ordination in the government with regard to this particular problem. No one has tried to tell us that there is no problem. One needs only to look at the pictures that appeared in the Globe and Mail last week and in the Parry Sound North Star, which is closely associated with the problem, to see that all the large wharves are right out of the water. You can walk around them on dry land. There is a problem, and no one has denied it.
But we have not seen that real concern about the problem which has brought about a cabinet group, or has brought the cabinet as a whole together to try to find an answer to it. We in the opposition have to try in the question period to ferret out from the government what they are doing and who is acting. We began by addressing our questions to the Minister of Public Works (Mr. Des-chatelets). The hon. member for Grey North (Mr. Noble) was persistent in his questioning for a number of weeks and we got very casual answers. Then we started to address our questions for a while to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing) because he is concerned with water resources as such. He answered our questions for a short time, until he made that unfortunate statement about praying for rain. We have not had an answer from him since.
When the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources seemed to be no longer connected with the problem we started to 20220-1831

If you cannot get answers or acceptance of responsibility from other ministers, then you ask the Prime Minister. The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin), because of his connection with the international joint commission, has made a number of incursions into this problem. He tabled a document, made an evasive answer and then withdrew leaving the field to some of his other colleagues. Canadian Water Resources or to whom we should address them. But certainly we have had no statement from either of these ministers.
In summary, there has been no collective or co-ordinated effort on the part of the government to deal with this problem. I do not know whether there is any cabinet committee. If there is not there certainly should be, but there has been no announcement in the house and no indication of any collective action. This is why we complain. If the problem is what they admit it is, then surely the Minister of Transport, the Minister of Public Works, the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources, the Secretary of State for External Affairs and any others who are essentially interested could get together and draw up a statement telling us what they are doing in order to relieve the minds of people in the tourist business, shipping and various other commercial enterprises. This they have not done. The whole system has broken down. As far as we can see, there is absolutely no coordinated effort. It seems to be a case of returning to the days when the Liberals were formerly in power, at which time each of the ministers attended to his own department and did not concern himself at all with the others. It appears that this is actually what is happening at this time.
We believe that the problem is not being regarded in a serious manner. We believe that the government is not looking for short or long term solutions to the problem. We have seen no evidence of it. We believe that the government has not co-ordinated its efforts along lines that are absolutely necessary, and that there has been a complete breakdown in the government's approach. We have, therefore, to make the strongest condemnation. We ask them to pull themselves together, to get going on this problem and to give the people some answers. Even if they cannot suggest an immediate solution, they should tell us that they are doing something and tell us what they are thinking about the various solutions I have mentioned, as well as other suggestions that have been made. The only suggestion from the United States authorities has been the grand canal project, and that is certainly a long way in the future. We do need this, it is true, but we also need some immediate action to alleviate the problem, not only this summer but next year as well.

That, in the interests of national development, this house urge the government to take concrete steps immediately to accelerate the application of ARDA.
That, Mr. Speaker, is relevant to the main motion which has left us a very narrow opening indeed. We will now be able to discuss a more particular point, the application of ARDA in the east as well as throughout Canada.
Let us now come to the point. There is in Canada at present a definite set of facts and economic situations. I shall relate all my remarks to that later on, but I should like to start with a few preliminary observations.
We are concerned over unemployment being rather high, but we are taking very weak action to alleviate it, as for instance the winter works program. This cannot really be called a planned or broad program to put an end to unemployment in our country. It is just like bringing coal to Newcastle, and that started a few years ago. Now we are giving Canadian citizens pick and shovel work in winter in order to lower unemployment.
However, there are causes to the unemployment situation. If we care to examine the problem closely, we will see that one of the causes is, partly, the stagnation of our agriculture at the present time.
I will give an example in my own region of Saguenay, many farmers are leaving their farms to go and find work in the city. This increases, nevertheless, the number of unemployed in our municipalities.
Here is another example. It is noted that in the province of Quebec there is, at St. Hilaire, a sugar beet factory which produces

a small percentage of the table sugar used in our province and in the country as a whole. Now, if we were to organize, within the framework of ARDA, other sugar beet industries, say, in the Saguenay area, the Gaspe peninsula and New Brunswick, then, a good many farmers of the surrounding districts could work and earn a substantial income from that product. At the same time these sugar beet industries could provide work for a number of city workers. This would at least alleviate unemployment and concrete results would be obtained in both cases. It would help some farmers and some unemployed to find work.
What is being done instead? Our sugar is bought somewhere else, when we would be able to produce large quantities of very good sugar in eastern Canada.
Previous governments, however, have always neglected agriculture, as known in eastern Canada, to consider exclusively the wheat problem. They forgot that there existed land capable of producing sugar beets, potatoes, onions, carrots and green peas, etc. Subsidies were given to western Canada only. Once again, we have nothing against these people out west who got those grants. But why not do the same thing in the eastern part of the country where crops are still more diversified?
If we had had more sugar beet factories, if that had been possible under ARDA, then our farmers and workers would really have been helped. Instead, we merely import our sugar from elsewhere, and since the troubles with Cuba-not us but our friends south of the border-we see the price of sugar rising tremendously and, once again, the Canadian consumer suffers the consequences.
Mr. Speaker, some people recently boasted -and this is a good illustration of what I am going to say-that there were signs of economic development, because some large corporations, like General Motors, had established themselves in the province of Quebec. But what about us in Quebec and Canada, in that context? We are only wage earners, employees, whereas foreign industrialists build up their business in this country, and remain its masters, getting the profits, and we poor Canadians always remain employees, wage earners in those foreign industries.
Mr. Speaker, that is the great drawback of our economic system. We are unable to assume our responsibilities and develop on our own, to remain the masters and owners of our natural wealth, of our industries and our
Canadian Water Resources trade. All we do is wait for some foreigners to settle here and do it instead.
I admit that the management of the General Motors Company has been bright enough, and had enough initiative to realize that there was a market for 100,000 cars a year in this country, and hastened to build this plant at Ste Therese de Blainville. Now, why should our economic system not allow us to build our own automobile industry, which we would own and control completely, so that we could have our own brands of cars, like many smaller countries, such as Belgium, Yugoslavia and Sweden?
I believe a sugar beet industry could easily be developed if we accelerated the program under ARDA. Had this been done in the past, had this program been applied throughout the country, secondary industries such as canning, could have been established, and the sugar beet industry could have been developed, along with others, and we would not be faced with this situation at the present time. Farmers are no longer able to live on their farms, they leave for the cities and overcrowd the labour market; they contribute to increased unemployment.
If we considered developing our economy in all sectors, in all fields, if we exerted ourselves to diversify it and profit by it, instead of waiting for foreigners to come and do it for us, then, we would be the masters. Why not try to produce at home what we can use, instead of importing? I remind you of the example I just gave, that of the sugar beet industry, which could be developed in the province of Quebec. At the present time, we produce only a small percentage of the sugar needed for Canadian consumption. We would be able to produce much more, and we would thereby avoid importing almost all the sugar we use in Canada.
Then, the farmers would work and enjoy a much happier life. They would have better living conditions and the number of unemployed would be reduced.
What I mean is that we do not feel capable of progressing by our own means. Let us do it ourselves.

On the other hand, a number of purely national industries, like the sugar beet industry which I just mentioned as an example, might be developed. As I say, of all our industries, the sugar beet industry is one with a national character; we have the raw material, and it could be developed and we would have a market for sugar.
All that should be installed, organized, put into operation as soon as possible, by accelerating, as it is requested in the motion, the application of ARDA, as provided in the act. Why is it not done? Because it seems that the government does not want to take long term, middle term or short term steps in the efforts it makes in all fields.
The policy of this government seems rather directed at alleviating certain conditions by half-measures, like for instance, winter works. Men are required to work with pick and shovel to build drainage systems, in order to give work to the greatest number of unemployed. That is the purpose of winter works. Why not put them all to work by giving them table spoons and putting machines and steam shovels in garages? Why are those men not used to build industries in the country, to build the country and develop it? There are claims to the effect that we need power developments, electric grids. Why not take our unemployed and put them to work on those projects according to a definite development program? In so doing, Canada would experience a rapid development, our economy would be put back on its feet and we would be doing Canadians a service. The government has only been able to find half-measures which are far from being the solution to the


development of this country. They simply tend to alleviate slightly the existing unemployment, and only in areas which are of benefit to but a few regions, such as with winter works. Where the climate is more severe, where snow stays longer than elsewhere, winter works are affected and those regions cannot benefit from the measure to the same extent as regions with a more temperate climate. The latter can derive much greater benefit than the former.
We do not approve this motion in its present form because the development of water resources comes under the provinces. To infringe upon that field would be to advocate centralization. It would accelerate centralization and transfer to Ottawa a sphere of exclusive provincial jurisdiction. For instance, paragraph (1) states the following:
-establishing a national advisory committee on water resources to assist in co-ordinating national resource development.
I say that watercourses do not come under the federal government but under the exclusive jurisdiction of the provinces.
Mr. Speaker, we believe that the government now has at its disposal an act which, if applied more elaborately, more rapidly and more extensively, could help to improve and strengthen our economy.
For instance, if ARDA was adapted to all areas of the country, in the east as well as the west, it could be useful. But, as I already said, it is not adapted as it should be. In western Canada it is easy to secure a $25,000 loan. I think that for a farmer with 1,000 acres of real estate, it is easy to secure a loan. On the other hand, in the province of Quebec the farmer has 100 acres only, but if these 100 acres are well developed, if the farmer uses modern machinery, he can produce as much, from the standpoint of value, as the western farmer who cultivates 1,000 acres but grows wheat only.
But today the Farm Credit Corporation lends much less to the eastern farmer, to the Quebec farmer. Why? Because the Quebec farmer has only 100 acres in land, whereas the western farmer has 1,000 acres, ten times more. Then, the eastern farmer gets a loan five times smaller.
And yet the eastern farmer can in all probability develop his land, get it to produce as economically as the western farmer whose farm covers 1,000 acres.
No help was given the eastern farmer to enable him to modernize his operation and put it on a more economic basis. That practice is not followed in eastern Canada. Why? Because the fact that eastern and western Canada go in for a different type of farming was not recognized.

I am happy to note that Canada enjoys such a diversified farm production. We produce wheat in the west, but we must also take into account the production potentialities of the east. That production might be extremely diversified, and I am glad of it, but I also think that we must pass legislation and accept principles, in short regulations, allowing all kinds of culture, and not the development of only one in quality and quantity.
The ARDA program is not achieving its purpose at the present time in the eastern part of our country because it is not adjusted to the type of farming which can be done there.

Some of these, particularly the consumptive uses, are becoming more demanding with the passage of time. Canadians have traditionally thought of water as a great source of energy, a source for the production of hydroelectric power; but increasingly it is becoming important for industrial purposes, for irrigation, for pollution control, process steam, and so on. These other needs are becoming more valuable. In many areas the usefulness of 20220-184
Canadian Water Resources water for power production purposes is still unchallenged, but in time this will certainly change.
Not only are these needs changing in character, and their nature becoming less oriented toward power production, but they are becoming crucial in widening areas of the country. A few decades ago there were only one or two spots in eastern Canada where water was in really short supply. This need has now extended to other areas. It is reaching the proportions of river basins. For example, the St. Lawrence river basin is now in some difficulty, and as these consumptive needs increase the effect of shortages will become more acute. This is a progessive development, not year by year because there are significant cyclical fluctuations but over the longer term; and certainly provision must be made to look after these requirements as they develop. They are moving from purely local problem areas to broader regional areas. In the United States they have become of great consequence from an inter-state point of view. They are becoming national in importance and I would underline the expectation that in the longer run they will also become of great concern on a continental basis. River basins will no longer be regarded as isolated one from the other; water diversions will be made from one area to another in order to relieve shortage. Surplus water areas literally hundreds of miles away from areas in which water is in short supply will be called upon to meet these increasingly valuable and urgent requirements.
I think one might look many years ahead and conceive what might be termed a broad continental approach to water development. If we look far enough into the future it would certainly seem unlikely that all our great northward flowing rivers would flow in their whole amount and uninterruptedly to the sea. Their flood waters, in part at least, will be turned southwards and redirected toward the areas of greatest requirement. They will be directed across the continent in an eastward direction as well as generally southwards. This water will be picked up at points of very high elevation and will swing down around the contours of the continent, so to speak, and used where it is most precious. This will happen earlier in the pre-Cambrian shield area. There is one minor diversion presently in existence, that of the Ogoki, whereby waters flowing into Hudson bay have been diverted ever since the early forties into lake Superior, and this has helped to relieve the initial problems of power production in that area and consumption problems in the great lakes area.

I should like to continue by painting briefly a picture of the type of diversion I have in mind. On the Harricanaw river there are freshets flowing into the James bay area during the late spring and early summer, none of which can be captured on site for power production. The great part of this water flows wastefully into the sea. How much better it would be to make use of this water by pumping it back to the divide in the Canadian shield and allowing it to flow into the great lakes system. Power which was, apparently, lost in the course of this operation could be recovered at Niagara falls and at the seaway plants. Thus, the power capacity which was involved near James bay at a very great distance from the main centres of consumption could be recovered ultimately at such points as Niagara and Lachine, where transmission difficulties are relatively slight and where the economics of distribution are much improved.
One can conceive in the fullness of time of water being brought from the northern part of British Columbia and from the Yukon to points further south where it is urgently needed. This is an area of high precipitation, a region where the winds coming across the Pacific drop most of their water burden. It

falls on those high mountains and, by and large, it flows to the sea through the Mackenzie and Yukon rivers. Great opportunities exist for diversions, by pumping and the building of canals, which would bring water down to the prairie provinces. As shortages develop in Alberta and central Saskatchewan, this water could be made progressively available in this way by diverting rivers such as the Athabasca and, subsequently, the Peace river. Later, the Liard and other rivers could be diverted, working backward to the great sources of water I have mentioned. This is one way in which use could be made of all the water that is picked up in the great areas of the Pacific and dropped in those northern mountain regions.
Later on it will be necessary to bring water in some quantity to the arid areas of the prairies. Conceivably, those diversions could be continued even to the great lakes basin. In other words, after decades of time and after the progressive evaluation of planned development, great schemes could be put in hand, not only for the diversion southward of water now running to the north but also for the diversion of water resources in British Columbia and the Yukon east across the prairies to the great lakes system. In this instance, as well, there is a need to put in energy in order to raise this water over divides. I would point out that it is possible to develop power plants earlier in those areas because there is an on-site need to do this. And it is possible to recover a large part of that energy in another place, notably in central Canada. Some of this pumping could be done in the northwest using fossil fuels; perhaps a use could be found for the vast quantities of energy which exists in the oil shale deposits of northern Alberta. There is even the possibility that this water flowing through canals, in some places, could serve as part of a transportation system, at least in summer.
So there is a multi-purpose aspect, here- water, energy production and transportation. Certainly, irrigation is a great consumptive requirement which will have to be met on the prairies, and provision will have to be made for the growing needs of southern Ontario, as well. There is, indeed, a whole field here, for exploration. Some of the projects which could be undertaken are small and are of relatively modest proportions. We should at least ensure that these individual projects fit into a broader plan for the optimum water resource development of this continent.
There is also the whole question of exporting water. I think we have to face this in much the same way as Canadians have belatedly faced the problem of exporting
Canadian Water Resources hydroelectric power. Once we commit ourselves to the long term export of water we cannot hope easily to repatriate this resource. It involves a service which moved flow into the factories and homes of thousands, even hundreds of thousands of people on the other side of the boundary. Thus, we have to be most careful about the such commitments. I think it is obvious that the only way to supplement the water supplies into the St. Lawrence system in a substantial manner is by diverting the waters which flow northward into James bay and Hudson bay. They are creating a fair amount of havoc in the north at the moment. They are contributing to the muskeg and to conditions which are not favourable to agriculture and the growth of harvestable forest cover. These diversions will, therefore, conceivably improve the prospects of the far north. But they will, inevitably, be associated with the United States because, by entering into a great watershed half of which is in Canada and half of which is in the United States, they will become more fully available to both countries.
We are faced with a special situation in the diversion of water at Chicago into the Mississippi. There are only a few feet of difference in elevation between lake Michigan and the upper tributaries of the Mississippi river system. Indeed, it only takes a shallow ditch to divert water from the St. Lawrence into the Mississippi. This was discovered years ago. At one time, more water flowed south from the St. Lawrence system into the Mississippi than is flowing today. The United States has from time to time considered making larger diversions but it has, in fact, limited those diversions. I believe the United States has behaved in a neighbourly manner in this respect when one considers that the value of this water and the useage to which it is being, and will be put, are rapidly increasing.
We have an opportunity here, I think, to capitalize on the moneys which could be raised for diversion purposes, and we must carefully assess the long term consequences of diverting rivers such as the Albany and the Severn which flow into Hudson bay so that part of this water would, perhaps, flow out to the Chicago diversion.
We must explore such matters as these in great depth and consider carefully all the contractual relationships involved before any commitments are entered into. Perhaps we have at hand a device by which the water shortages of southern Ontario can be solved along with the water problems of those states of the United States which border the great lakes. In the case of power, different ways

More important still to Canada, I think, is the fact that they could be raised at lower interest rates than are generally available in Canada and certainly to individual Canadian provincial governments or utilities. They will be offered in effect at very low interest rates and their very size will reflect in part the lowness of the interest rate. speechtext: Mr. Speaker, there should be no surprise on the part of the Canadian people that such a state of affairs exists. While hon. members opposite have, as I said in my initial remarks, called for a polarization of debate I would simply like to say-I have said it many times and I say it this afternoon with a stronger voice than I have ever used before-that the party of centralization bases its activities on the doctrines so often expounded by the Secretary of State, bases its activities on the Pearson plan, and on the book called "Troubled Canada". I ask all hon. members if they will not admit that the Pearson plan, the book by the Secretary of State, and the book by the Minister of Finance are all exposes, if you will, of the doctrine of centralization. Let us stop trying to bring red herrings into this debate; let us put our cards on the table.

Mr. Speaker, at the outset of my remarks before six o'clock, I stated that if our Conservative government, under the leadership of the then prime minister (Mr. Diefenbaker), was really successful in the field of resources, it was because our Conservative government had readily realized the necessity of cooperating with the provinces. That is why we were successful in our ARDA policies, as well as in the setting up of a council of resources ministers.

Mr. Speaker, I repeat, as I did at the outset of my remarks before six o'clock, that if the

government I supported had success in the resources field, in the field of ARDA, it was because our government, supported by a party and directed by a prime minister who knew the true meaning and spirit of co-operation with the provinces, brought these things into being. I would like to state again that I believe there has been a slowing down of the momentum in these programs. Why? Again I say, because the party of centralization has been basing its activities on the doctrines so often expounded by the Secretary of State (Mr. Lamontagne) and on the Pearson plan. Far too many people blame the ministers, but it is the Pearson plan that is underlined by a high notion of centralization which cannot be applied to the facts of federal life in 1964. This government has been basing its activities on the book called "Troubled Canada", and all these ideas expound the glories of centralization and leave no room for any idea of co-operative federalism; there is no room for any idea of co-operation with the provinces.
Why then, we should ask ourselves, has there been failure in planning for resources by the government that sits opposite? It is just not an accident; it is because they have based their governmental activities on the doctrines of centralization, which they are doing their best to disown but which they cannot disown.
I say the Liberal government's failure under the Pearson plan, its failure in policy in the field of resources, is based on the same reason for their having failed in all their economic activities as a government. It is because they have failed to consult with the provinces; they have failed to consult with local authorities; they have failed, as ministers, even to consult among themselves. One minister makes one sort of speech on economic planning, another minister makes another sort of speech. I often wonder whether Mr. Kent vets these speeches out, or whether he should not start doing so pretty soon. At any rate, Mr. Speaker, this government might mouth the glories of co-operative federalism, but they do not believe in co-operative federalism.
The next remark I want to make is this, Mr. Speaker. I have made it very often before inside and outside this House of Commons. The right hon. Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) is surrounded on the treasury benches by some very senior and very able ex-senior bureaucrats. I happen to be one of those-and I am not just saying this to flatter-who think that we Canadians are blessed with one of the finest of civil services in the world. But the right hon. Prime Minister, an ex-senior bureaucrat himself is surrounded by whom, and from whom does
Canadian Water Resources he take his advice? He takes it from the Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) and his book "Troubled Canada". Does this not underline the glories of centralization? The Prime Minister takes his advice from the Secretary of State, (Mr. Lamontagne) who wrote one of the great exposes on the glories of centralization and who just the other day, because he thought it was convenient, did a somersault and said, "You know, ladies and gentlemen, that was in the province of Quebec. I think, after all, that decentralization is really a very good thing for federalism".
There is a senator in the other place who said just a few years ago that his party, the Liberal party, was wallowing in the quagmires of pragmatism. Well, Mr. Speaker, they cannot turn somersaults and get away with it that easy while we are in the opposition. Our successes in these fields were based, again I say, on the principles of our party. Those who surround the Prime Minister today have shown time and time again that this notion of centralization cannot be applied to the facts of federal life in 1964. From whom does the Prime Minister take his counsel in regard to economic matters? We have seen that the Pearson plan and the right hon. Prime Minister himself are dominated by the centralizers. This leaves no room for the party that forms this government to advance sincerely any notion on co-operative federalism with the provinces.
With many other Canadians I rejoiced the other day when it seemed that the Prime Minister (Mr. Pearson) attained a certain amount of agreement with the province of Quebec with relation to the pension plan. I rejoiced, as I think did every other hon. member, thinking of the old people of our country and putting country before party. But what about all this nonsense that the premier of Quebec and the Prime Minister of Canada have saved confederation? I ask you, Mr. Speaker, if a friend and I were to set fire to a house and we watched it bum, and then just before the house was almost destroyed we called in the fire brigade and with the fire brigade we saved that house, could we honestly be credited with saving the house? The Prime Minister with his centralist activities nearly sabotaged national unity and the spirit of co-operative federalism, which is so necessary to put programs like this into operation. The Minister of Finance (Mr. Gordon) added a little gas to the fire and the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss LaMarsh) added a little more gas to the fire. Then they called in the fire brigade, and all the Liberals in Canada stood up and said they had saved confederation. This is just so much palpable nonsense.

The facts of life, Mr. Speaker, are that Mr. Rene Levesque, realizing that Liberalism in the province of Quebec does not say the same thing as Liberalism here in Ottawa, which is based on the centralist approach, is demanding the separation of the Liberal party in Quebec from the federal wing. There is no other reason-
