speechtext: Order. I am wondering if the hon. member does not feel as the Chair is inclined to feel, that he is digressing to some extent from the motion before the house.

Well, Mr. Speaker, I am trying to develop the theme that most Canadians are beginning to realize, that it is not just an accident that the Liberals are not having success with getting action on economic programs, such as the ARDA program and resource programs, because their whole system of activity is based on the idea of centralization, which cannot be put into effect today. While it might seem that I am getting out of order, I am relating my remarks to the subject before the house today in an attempt to show why the government are experiencing such failures.
I think that spokesmen for the government in Ottawa as well as spokesmen-I hope I am not out of order in saying this-for the government of Quebec are doing national unity and the future of our country great disservice when they confuse-I will not say intentionally, but if it happens too often in the future I shall have to say intentionally- ordinary, every day problems concerning provincial rights with the problems of bilingualism and biculturalism. I submit that in many ways they are two distinct things. I think the present government of Quebec and the government at Ottawa are doing a great disservice to this country if and when they intentionally confuse these two matters.
In relation to federal-provincial relations, Mr. Speaker, we are told by many people that all of a sudden the present government have a new plan. They are going to come to the House of Commons and put forward legislation, and then after consulting with the provinces, etc., they are going to be willing to amend this clause, that clause, and so on. I am not going to argue that a certain amount of this under present day conditions is not necessary, but I am going to say that this is no excuse for the past performance of this government in regard to federal-provincial relations. This government has put legislation time and time again before this House of Commons without any consultation with the provinces, and subsequently they have wondered why their whole [Mr. Graiftey.l
economic program, including resource planning which we are discussing today, has floundered on the rocks. It has floundered on the rocks because they do not believe deeply in co-operative federalism; they only talk about it. I ask the Secretary of State how he, having written an expose on federalism a few years ago, can suddenly adopt overnight the Conservative principle of decentralization and at the same time keep a straight face?
Have you read the book?

Yes, I have, and in many instances 1 congratulate the minister for writing a very interesting and good book. But if the minister's mind really turned a somersault overnight I cannot congratulate him either for his sincerity or his pragmatism. This new idea of introducing legislation in this House of Commons without consultation with the provinces and then saying that the government are willing to amend it in the spirit of co-operative federalism is just a pure lack of preparation.
In closing my remarks, Mr. Speaker, I should like to stress something that I have often stressed in this house before with regard to the problem we have at hand. I do not believe that this government are going to make any advances in the field of resource or water planning, in the field of ARDA, or in the field of any economic activity, unless they improve relationships with the provinces immediately. Without improved relationships with the provinces there will be no improvement in the situation mentioned by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) this afternoon. It must be realized that the Canadian constitution is the first constitution in the world which combines a federal system of government with a parliamentary system. A federal system of government seeks to combine a measure of unity with a measure of diversity. I should like to quote a remark made by the late Right Hon. Mackenzie King after the publication of the Rowell-Sirois report. He remarked:
This arrangement of continuity and permanence is necessary, because co-operation between the dominion and other provinces is too vital a matter to be left entirely for intermittent conferences and to correspondence between governments.
Mr. King made this remark after the government of Nova Scotia at a prior federal-provincial conference had spoken out regarding the necessity for the establishment of more sophisticated approaches to federal-provincial affairs; after the province of Nova Scotia had spoken out for the necessity of creating a permanent secretariat for federal-provincial affairs. What did the Rowell-Sirois

report have to say on this subject, Mr. Speaker? It said:
But co-operation between autonomous governments is difficult to achieve. Administrative authorities responsible to different legislatures are not always interested in co-operation; indeed, non-co-operation may on occasion serve their immediate interests.
Autonomous governments may thus tend to become rival centres of power rather than agencies for co-operative pursuit of the public weal.
I do not pretend that the problem facing the present government is an easy one to solve. But I am saying this: It will have to initiate and adopt more sophisticated measures than have been used up till now; it will have to create, or help to create, more sophisticated bodies for the guidance of federal-provincial relations than any which exist at present if any headway is to be made in economic planning or the planning of resources, such as we are discussing this evening.
The Rowell-Sirois report, in dealing with this aspect of the subject, states:
There may be certain disadvantages in not having a single department in each government charged with the responsibility for inter-governmental communications. Each province must, of course, decide for itself the expediency of establishing such a department, but the commission is inclined to think that the delay and inconvenience of having the voluminous correspondence, which is today necessary between governments, conducted by one department would make the suggested innovation undesirable.
The commission goes on to recommend the establishment of a permanent secretariat, and I believe that although the Prime Minister has taken upon himself responsibility for federal-provincial relations, the initiative shown up to this point has not been sufficient. I understand initiative has been shown by certain departments of government, among them the Department of Labour. I understand that certain officials in various departments have been in contact with their counterparts in the provincial governments. This is commendable, but it is not good enough. I repeat: A permanent secretariat for federal-provincial relations must be set up on the premiers and Prime Minister level; otherwise the federal government in its dealings with the provinces will go from one crisis to another, and they might as well forget about planning in the field of resources, the field of ARDA, or any other economic venture.
Hon. gentlemen opposite should put first things first and get on with this job. It is all very well to have reached an agreement a few days ago regarding pensions with the province of Quebec. But at what price? The minister laughs; but I happen to live in the province of Quebec and I know what takes place when we have Liberal governments in Quebec and in Ottawa saying one thing inside
Canadian Water Resources the province and another thing outside it. Yes, "conscription if necessary, but not necessarily conscription"-I am not too young to remember that; and hon. members opposite are doing the same things today. Before an agreement was reached on pensions, this country was divided as it never was before. Mr. Levesque knows that; he realizes Liberalism means one thing in Ottawa and another in the province of Quebec.
Same old bunch.

I know some hon. members thought I was getting off the subject, but I am dealing now with one of the reasons for the failure of the government in the fields of economic and resource planning. They think all the wisdom resides here in Ottawa and that the centralizers and the ex-bureaucrats have all the answers. But that is not true. While we rejoice in the arrangement made in the pension field, unless such a secretariat as I have mentioned is established, and established soon, the Prime Minister has simply stuck a little band aid over a major wound. Unless co-operative federalism is not merely preached but sincerely put into operation, confederation will suffer again as soon as we are confronted with further provincial problems. I think most Canadians realize this.
I know that in debating this subject this evening I have gone far afield. I believe the observations I have made in entering into this debate could be repeated from time to time with a direct bearing on most of the activities of the present government. The government has already failed dismally to show any initiative toward improving the economy of this nation, and if hon. members opposite are sincere in their protestations about co-operative federalism they will soon make sure that the former senior bureaucrats, and those others who have the Prime Minister's ear, change their notions about relations with the provinces. I say this not only in a partisan sense but as a young Canadian who is interested in the unity of this country in the future. Rather than stumble from crisis to crisis with the provinces it is time the government did some long range thinking and began at least to initiate the establishment of a secretariat along the lines I have advocated.

The hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) has rendered the house a service by directing the attention of the chamber to this very important question of the need for a water conservation policy in Canada.
We have been very slow in Canada in recognizing that water is a commodity of basic importance to our economy. It is essential,
2902	HOUSE OF
Canadian Water Resources as hon. members know, for the generation of hydroelectric power, for industrial development, for domestic use and for recreational purposes. On occasions, it has even been used for drinking purposes as a last resort. Our friends to the south, in the United States, were much quicker to recognize how important water is. In this northern half of the continent we pride ourselves on having almost limitless supplies of water and we have done very little to conserve our water resources. But during the same period the Americans, who had gone through the industrial revolution much earlier than we, became aware of the fact that the growth of their economy was largely dependant on the supply of water which could be made available to the great urban and industrial centres. This is why during the 'thirties, while we were keeping roughly a million people on relief in Canada, the Americans spent hundreds of millions of dollars building some of the largest dams in the world both for the purpose of water conservation and for the generation of hydroelectric power.
Since the war, the Americans have used their army engineers to work with the state governments to launch tremendous water conservation projects in almost every part of the country. They have piped water hundreds of miles in order to turn their deserts into gardens and make possible the extension of their urban communities and the establishment of new industries in places where it would not be possible without adequate supplies of water. But we in this country are only beginning to appreciate the problem. If anyone had told us 20 years ago that in the southern part of Ontario, surrounded by the great lakes and close to Niagara Falls, the day would come when we would be threatened with a water shortage, such a person would have been laughed to scorn. The fact is that the problem is already upon us and it will increase with the passing of the years. There is a drastic need for the government of Canada in conjunction with the provinces of Canada to work out water conservation and water usage programs.
The amendment which the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) has moved draws our attention to the fact that there is an imminent national crisis in water resource management and it makes reference to three things: First, the low levels of the great lakes; second, the increasing pollution of national waters and, third, the need for a conservation of resources program. May I say a word about each of those very briefly.
The question of the critical low water levels of the great lakes is, of course, of tremendous importance to the provinces of Ontario and EMr. Douglas.]

Quebec, not only because of the supplies of water for domestic purposes but because the great lakes have become the great inland transportation network of industrial Canada. The necessity of doing something about water levels on the great lakes is something which I am sure no one needs to stress in this house.
The matter of water pollution is a subject which has been long neglected. We are polluting most of the rivers in Canada and a number of lakes. It is hard to believe that in this age of sanitary engineering there are cities in Canada which are still discharging raw sewage into our rivers and lakes, polluting our water resources and killing fish. Industrial effluents are being poured into our national waters which are having a damaging effect on the use of the water for livestock and other purposes.
This amendment asks the house to condemn the neglect of the government in failing to establish a co-ordinated national water policy and for ignoring the national crisis in water resources management. I do not know, Mr. Speaker, how we can select this particular administration for condemnation. I think each successive government in Canada has been negligent in dealing with this matter. Both this administration and the previous one have been negligent.
The first move that was made to conserve water was taken back in the 1930's when Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner, minister of agriculture in the administration of Right Hon. W. L. Mackenzie King, introduced the Prairie Farm Rehabilitation Act. Under this legislation a very good staff was built up over the years. They did excellent work on the prairies by helping farmers to establish small dugouts for their livestock. They built a number of small dams which had very beneficial effects on the prairies. This organization could have done much better work had it been given more money, but I think credit must go to it and particularly to the former director, the late L. B. Thomson, for the work which was done and for the foundation that was laid for a much broader program which has not yet materialized.
P.F.R.A. and its staff laid the groundwork for considering the South Saskatchewan river development project. Here I think that credit has to go to the previous administration under the leadership of the present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker). For 20 years the Liberal government had talked about the South Saskatchewan dam. In the 1945 election the Liberal party went so far as to say: We have the money, we have the men and as soon as the material is available we will begin to build the South Saskatchewan dam. But 10 years later, although the money and the

men and the material were all available, nothing had been done about building the dam.
I have some rather unhappy memories of those days when the federal government kept saying to the provincial government: If you will just offer to contribute a little more to this project we can go ahead. In spite of repeated offers an agreement was never signed. I give credit to the government of the present Leader of the Opposition in that when they came to office we were able to negotiate an agreement and work was started on the South Saskatchewan dam.
Lest members from other parts of Canada go away with the idea that the federal government is paying all the cost, I think I should point out that when that project is completed the people of the province of Saskatchewan will be paying a little better than 60 per cent of the total cost and the government of Canada will be paying about 40 per cent.
Oh, come off it.
Did somebody say "come off it"?
Are you speaking of the building of the dam?

My friend from Rosetown-Biggar knows the story very well and he can be sure I will give all the facts, if he will just sit still. On the building of the main reservoir the federal government is putting up 75 per cent of the cost and the provincial government 25 per cent. But this represents only in the neighbourhood of $100 million while the total cost of the project will run to well over $165 million. When the hydro installations are put in, when the ground is levelled, when the canals are built, when the lateral ditches are installed, when the land is prepared for irrigation and the ancillary works to take water into the Qu'Appelle valley are completed, the people of Saskatchewan will have put up better than 60 per cent of the total cost of the whole project.
I say that for the information of members from other parts of Canada. I do not say it to detract in any way from the generosity of the federal government in proceeding with the project. I am convinced that the construction of the dam will be a turning point in the economic life of the prairies and particularly western Saskatchewan because it will make possible not only irrigated land on which there can be diversification of crops, the growing of sugar beets, the building of sugar factories, market gardening, canneries, quick freezing units, but it will also mean backing water up into the hills so that in many areas livestock can be raised where
Canadian Water Resources they could not be raised before because of lack of water. It will make possible urban growth, recreational facilities and industrial development. In my opinion it will be a great forward step in western Saskatchewan and, indeed, in all of western Canada because the South Saskatchewan dam will back water up for 142 miles so that there will be a great lake 142 miles long and about five miles wide. The effect of that body of water cutting across the Palliser triangle will be tremendous so far as the climatic conditions in that semi-arid plain are concerned. I give full marks to the government of that time for proceeding with that project.
I give them credit also for the resources for tomorrow conference which was well organized and well conceived. It brought together a number of top flight people across Canada who were concerned about the problem of resource conservation. I think that out of the conference there came many good ideas and the foundation was laid for a real attack on this problem. Out of this conference came the idea of ARDA which also was a worth-while concept.
However, Mr. Speaker, when you have said that you have said it all. A conference, in itself, does not conserve resources. The ARDA program, although it contains the germ of a good idea, has not yet produced any great projects to deal with the problem that has been raised in this amendment. I therefore return to my thesis that none of the governments of Canada have really tackled this problem. To blame the present administration, which has been in office for about 12 months, it seems to me is something like the pot calling the kettle black.
I believe that instead of trying to apportion blame, and I am not trying to do that, we have to recognize that both the major parties have made some obeisances to the need for doing something about water conservation but we have never, in Canada, tackled this problem on anything like the scale on which it needs to be approached. We have not even closely approximated what our friends in the United States have done, even having due regard to the difference in population and financial resources of these two countries. Apart from the South Saskatchewan dam, we really have not done anything of major proportions about conserving some of the great water resources of this country.
We have done nothing at all about river pollution-neither this Liberal government nor the Liberal government that was in power for 22 years or the Conservative government that was in office for some six years. None of them did anything about this question of river pollution. I recognize the necessity for

Canadian Water Resources the co-operation of the provinces and municipalities in connection with this problem. We cannot continue to pollute the national waters of this country without paying for it and our children and our children's children will pay for poisoning of our rivers and our lakes with industrial effluents and raw sewage. Unless we tackle this problem fairly soon, the bill will be delivered in the not too distant future.
When we speak of water conservation- and members on both sides of the house paid tribute to the value of conserving water- it seems to me somewhat ironical that the party that has moved this amendment and the party against whom it is directed have both entered into an agreement to turn over the entire flow of the Columbia river to the United States. This is the fourth largest river on the North American continent, and we have not only allowed the United States to determine the flow of that river, the extent to which water will be diverted from it, but we have actually limited ourselves for the life of the agreement in connection with our right to divert water.
This afternoon the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) talked about our right to the consumptive use of water from the Columbia. He said, we cannot take it exclusively for the generation of hydroelectric power. I asked him where he found the word "exclusively", and he said some lawyers told him it was there. He said he was not a lawyer, and neither am I, but I know that no lawyer, by even the most subtle interpretation, can put a word there that is not there. Article 1 of the treaty, clause (e) defines consumptive use. It says:
(e) "Consumptive use" means use of water for domestic, municipal, stock-water, irrigation, mining or industrial purposes but does not include use for the generation of hydroelectric power;
The protocol which was supposed to rectify this situation contains nothing but mild generalities and says:
Canada and the United States are in agreement that article XIII (1) of the treaty provides to each of them a right to divert water for a consumptive use.
In other words, water can be diverted but only for the purposes which I read a moment ago from clause (e). It can be diverted for irrigation or municipal purposes, but it cannot be diverted if the generation of hydroelectric power is involved. As every member knows, in this modern age it is uneconomical to divert water except for a multi-purpose project, and the only thing that makes possible a large scale diversion is the use of water for several purposes. You can use it to develop power, pass it through the turbines and use it for stock-watering, for irrigation, for

domestic and industrial purposes. Unless it can be used for all of these purposes, then it becomes uneconomic to divert water. Here are two parties, one of whom drafted the agreement and the second is now in the process of putting it through the house, who pay lip service to water conservation, and in the same breath they give away one of the greatest assets in this country, the tremendous volume of water which we have at hand. Before long we shall be condemned for this failure to discharge properly our stewardship in looking after these resources, of which we are only the trustees.
Someone sent me a rather interesting clipping from the Phoenix Gazette, printed in Phoenix, Arizona under date of April 7, 1964, which tells of a meeting in Arizona in which the engineers and other experts were concerned about how they were going to get enough water in Arizona. I quote:
It was agreed that the 1.2 million acre feet which could be provided by the central Arizona project from the Colorado river would still leave the state with a water deficit of almost two million acre feet a year. Better water conservation practices could wipe out some of the deficit, but long range planning indicates the need for a larger and more permanent source of water, it was noted.
Then the article goes on to outline how they hope to get enough water down in Arizona.
It says:
So this leaves outside sources, and while officially no one would say just where these sources might be, privately some agreed that the huge Columbia river probably would hold best promise of a future supply. Water experts have said the state might possibly get up to 12 million acre feet annually from such a source.
Then it says:
The Columbia river is in the Pacific northwest.
Well, I do not suppose the people in Arizona care whether it is in the Pacific northwest or not, or whether it is going to come from Canada. What they are concerned about is that they get 12 million acre feet of water a year sent across the line into the United States, with no controls whatever as to how it is used, how it is diverted and where it is diverted to; whereas on the Canadian side we are going to have our hands tied, and are going to wait for the next 60 years with this valuable resource pouring across the line, at 90 million cubic feet per second, into the United States.
This debate has been concerned with the matter of water resource management, and I had expected someone from the government side would tell us what the government's policy is going to be with respect to water. So far the only statement was that

by the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis), who is the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister, and I hope to heaven he was not speaking for the government because he outlined a great program of diverting our rivers from northern B.C. and northern Ontario down south, for the purpose of exporting water and selling it to the United States.
They used to have a saying in the army, "If it moves, salute it, and if it does not move, paint it." The Liberals seem to have a slogan, "If it is profitable, export it." They seem to look upon Canada as a great source of raw material, from which we will export pulpwood, oil, minerals, aluminum, gas, electric power and water. Last year we exported nearly 40,000 people to the United States.
I would like to think of Canada, not as a country of only 20 million people, developing extraction industries to sell raw material to the United States where it can be made into manufactured products and shipped back to us, but of Canada some day being a nation of tens of millions of people, using its energy resources, its water resources and its natural resources to develop not only extraction industries but secondary and tertiary industries to retain employment opportunities in this country, and to develop a great nation. No country ever became a great nation by being merely a hewer of wood and a drawer of water.
I must confess that when I listened to the parliamentary secretary to the Prime Minister this afternoon I was absolutely frightened at the prospect that now, in addition to exporting power and raw materials, we are going to set about exporting the great water resources of our country. Surely we, as Canadians, have got more imagination and a greater sense of reality than to think that the only use that can be made of the resources of the country is to see how quickly we can get rid of them.
I had hoped that the government would give the house the benefit of its ideas with regard to what it was going to do about water conservation and utilization. Up to now we certainly have had no intimation as to what the government's policy is.
I do not join in condemning the government for the fact that it has failed to establish a co-ordinated national water policy and ignored the imminent crisis in water resource management. It has only been in office about a year. These are problems which have gone on for a long time, but I think the house is entitled to a statement from the responsible ministers as to what the government is going
Canadian Water Resources to do, in the course of the next few years, about our water resources. I hope they will tell us something better than the statement made this afternoon, that all we can think of doing about our water resources is export them to the United States. The only consoling thing about the statement of the hon. member for Coast-Capilano was what he said about it taking decades of time. The Liberal party always seems to think in geological terms of time, and I think that is why it is moving as slowly as the glaciers.
It probably will not happen quickly, but I seriously ask the government to formulate a policy, because time is important. Already in the great lakes area of southern Ontario water is a problem. On the prairies water is a problem. The prairies have now reached a maximum of agricultural production under dry farming methods. If there is to be increased agricultural production on the prairies more water is a necessity. The big crops of the past two or three years were due to the fact that rain came at the right time. If it were possible on the prairies to have, not irrigation, but a sprinkler system through plastic or aluminum pipes, so that a very small amount of water could be sprinkled on the fields at exactly the right time, production per acre could be increased by five or eight bushels.
Water is vital to the future development of the country. Fortunately we have great resources of water, more water than our friends to the south, and that is why our friends to the south would be very happy to spend a few billion dollars in Canada if they could get access to our water resources. But if we are going to build a country that will have a great future we must plan how to regulate our water resources, how to make water available to the areas that need it, and how to keep free from pollution the great national waters which constitute the life blood of our country and its economy.
I hope the government will not treat this question lightly. I do not offer words of condemnation but I make an urgent appeal to the government to take action very quickly in setting up the kind of machinery by which the provincial governments and the federal government can sit down and plan a water conservation policy, map out the necessary programs, and then find the required financial resources to put those programs into effect.
This country will grow only as fast as it is able to make water available to a growing and expanding economy. I hope the government will rise to the challenge and, if it does, it will have the gratitude of future generations. If it does nothing about it, and we continue to drift, with water levels dropping,

Canadian Water Resources with large areas of Canada in a semi-arid condition, then those who come after us will feel we have been very poor trustees of the responsibilities given to us by our forefathers.
The hon. member has talked about a planned economy. I would like to ask him how socialist planning would prevent the exporting of our wheat and grain to communist China and Russia?

I have never objected to exporting. Any country lives by exporting. There is a great deal of difference between exporting wheat or exporting shoes or lumber on the one hand, and exporting things we need in our own country, such as supplies of water, gas and electric power especially if those resources can be used in Canada to turn our raw materials into finished products. We can turn our raw materials into finished products and export them. I do not quarrel with exporting surplus goods to the United States or any other country; as a matter of fact, we must do that in order to live. But my contention is that for too long Canada has been content to develop extraction industries which give employment to relatively few people per million dollars of capital investment, to ship these raw materials to the United States, to ship to the United States the energy and electric power to turn those raw materials into finished products, and then to buy them back.
I think we could use those same resources in Canada, manufacture the finished product and then export it. What we have been doing, really, is exporting jobs. I think we ought to start exporting finished products or semi-processed products wherever that is possible.

Mr. Speaker, I wonder
whether the hon. gentleman would permit one further question. I may be mistaken, but I thought I heard him say that P.F.R.A. was introduced under the government of the Right Hon. Mackenzie King. It is my impression, although perhaps I am mistaken, that P.F.R.A., although perhaps under another name, was introduced by the Bennett government.

Mr. Speaker, perhaps I did not make myself clear. The legislation was introduced in the last year the Bennett government was in office, but the administration was set up mainly by the Right Hon. J. G. Gardiner.

Mr. Speaker, we welcome this opportunity on a supply motion to have the leader of the official opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) select the subject matter for a two-day debate. I think this is one of six supply motions that must come before the house, and it is a very

welcome opportunity for some of the members of the opposition, particularly the Leader of the Opposition, to determine what the subject matter for that two-day debate shall be. Having said that, it seems to me they have successfully moved an amendment pointing to a very serious problem in Canada and then the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) and the hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) have proceeded to actually condemn the administration that was set up under their own government during the years in which they had the power to do something about the problem raised in the amendment.
I say that, Mr. Speaker, because the third point they raise in the amendment is this:
-vigorously continuing and expanding the water and other resource development programs conceived and established by the previous Conservative government.
If there had been resource development programs actually established and under way to retain the water levels in the great lakes, I suggest that the first part of their amendment would not be valid. That is to say, they condemn the government of today for "ignoring the imminent national crisis in water resources management, which is evidenced by the critical low water levels of the great lakes"; and surely no reasonable member would suggest that the critical low levels of water in the great lakes today is something that has happened in the last few months. Surely if there had been satisfactory programs established such as the amendment says, this problem would not have been before us today. I join with the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas) in suggesting that these problems which are facing Canada today, and which are accurately described, I think, as amounting to an "imminent national crisis in water resources management", are something for which the immediately preceding government will have to shoulder the blame as well as the present government.
Getting back to the question of water, Mr. Speaker, and the preservation and conservation of our water resources, I think it is well for us to consider the position of Canada today in relation to the water resources that we have, and also to rely on some of the experiences other nations have had, so that we can in fact look into the future and develop programs that will help Canada to avoid these other problems. I think that one of the first requirements in developing a national water resources program is to accept the statement that was made by Kenneth Holum, assistant secretary of the interior for water and power in the United States. He says this:

Experts estimate that our needs for water will triple by the year 2000.
This is the United States. Then he goes on to say this:
One thing, however, that there would be no more of, is water. The aggregate amount of water in the rivers, streams and lakes, in the underground aquifers, in the clouds floating across the skies, and in the seas and oceans would be substantially the same as it is today.
That is in the year 2000. Then he says:
We can't produce more water. Our job is to use what we have. We have to learn to use the water we are wasting, and to use it over and over and over again. We must do a better job of maintaining quality, so that water can be reused, and improve the quality of poor water so that it is usable.
The United States have come to some pretty agonizing conclusions respecting this matter of using the water which they have, and it is interesting to note the price that they put on water today. For example, in the issue of the Christian Science Monitor of March 18, 1964, there is an article captioned "Water for everyone" which says this:
The problem is that nature's water system just doesn't coincide with human requirements, says a world famous geophysicist as he describes the research frontiers this presents in the last of ten articles on "on the water challenge passed by growing water needs of the United States.
In this article he quotes Nathaniel Wollman of the University of New Mexico and says:
Nathaniel Wollman.. .has concluded that the money worth of water in the United States adds up like this:
This is all over the United States:
Industry-$3,000 to $4,000 per acre-foot.
Recreation-$250 per acre-foot.
Agriculture-$51 per acre-foot.
If you compare that with some of the water resources that are available in Canada today, it certainly points up the fact that we had better look after these resources now.
During the course of the debate which took place in this house on March 5 mention was made of a report of a study made by the engineering firm of Crippen-Wright. I think this survey and report was paid for by the government of Saskatchewan and it dealt with the cost of diverting some of the water now running into the Arctic ocean and Hudson bay from the southern prairies. It was pointed out that to divert water from the North Saskatchewan river and the Clearwater river into the South Saskatchewan river through the Red Deer river would cost about 40 cents per acre foot. Compare that, Mr. Speaker, with the value which the United States puts on water of $51 per acre foot. In addition to that, there was a second possible diversion, which was to divert the Athabasca into the North Saskatchewan, and I think subsequently into the South Saskatchewan as well through the Red Deer river,
Canadian Water Resources at a cost of $1.60 per acre foot, making available 4,500,000 acre feet. A third possible diversion was from the Peace river into the North Saskatchewan which would allow 19 million acre feet to be developed at a cost of $2.70 per acre foot. Then there was a fourth possible diversion from the upper Fraser into the Athabasca at a cost of $3.10 per acre foot, making available for development 1,090,000 acre feet. The fifth in order of cost was the possibility of diverting 5,430,000 acre feet from the Columbia at a cost of $4.60 per acre foot.
That is the gross cost?

Yes, gross cost, that is correct.
One other very important program in Canada which could be undertaken and which has not yet been touched, and which I suggest is cheaper than any of the diversions referred to in the report I mentioned, is the building of upper level storage on the eastern slopes of the Rocky mountains. Outside of some very small reservoirs on the Bow river there are no dams and no storage facilities provided in the upper regions of any of our rivers coming through the eastern slopes of the Rocky mountains. I know that shortly there will be in the Peace river dam, but on the tributaries of the North Saskatchewan river and on the South Saskatchewan river there are, outside of the Bow river, absolutely no storage facilities or what is called upper storage. There are sites which I think are reasonably cheap in terms of cost and development, at which large storage facilities could be built at a cost of even less than 40 cents per acre foot, which is the cheapest of the diversions to which I referred.
We in southern Alberta have had quite a lot of experience with irrigation. I think that today most of the irrigation projects in western Canada which have been undertaken -that is, the major irrigation projects-are in fact located in southern Alberta. We know there are times, such as in May and June when there are large flows of water, when we simply have to let this water go by because we do not have any storage facilities to contain it. This water is water which flows naturally into river basins without diversion of any sort. We also know that it is impossible for us to divert into irrigation reservoirs even 10 per cent of this water when it goes by in the months of May and June during the high run-off period.
Therefore I want to put this very positive proposal to the government. I suggest that one of the first undertakings with regard to water conservation should be the large scale development of upper storage on the eastern slopes of the Rocky mountains. I say that because whenever water is stored at its

Canadian Water Resources highest position it is obvious that everyone downstream can make optimum use of that water for all purposes. It can be used for irrigation; by municipalities which rely on these rivers for water, as well as providing a uniform flow of water for hydroelectric generation. In my opinion that is the most important project which should be the first to be undertaken.
Following that consideration should be given to some of these diversions of water into areas which require it. However, it appears to me that it will be 40, 50 or perhaps 60 years before we will be able to utilize all of the natural flow which runs down the South Saskatchewan river even now. This water will have to be conserved on a 12-month basis, because something like seven million acre feet of water flows annually down that river at the present time. I am not quite sure of those figures but I think that more than four fifths of that water escapes us during the high flow season when we simply do not have the storage to make use of it.
If I may turn for a moment to the question of the utilization of this water, I want to say to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquitlam (Mr. Douglas), and to other hon. members who may think that building a large irrigation system and building large structures necessary to deliver the water to the land means that you have reached the point where you are going to have a lot of prosperous farmers, that we have found over the years that we run into very serious difficulties, particularly during the first 20 or 25 years, in getting farmers to make proper use of this water. As far as their growing grain, cereals and other crops is concerned, compared with the lower cost of operation of dry land farming they have felt that these units are economic failures. The day may come 50 or 60 years from now when the value of cereal grains and the market for cereal grains will be such that they can be successfully and profitably grown on acres which are under the ditch. But that is not true today. We know there are crops which can be grown successfully and profitably, such as sugar beets, vegetable crops and a certain amount of beef and dairy production, in irrigated areas of southern Alberta. There are some very serious problems, however, in the marketing of these crops which have not as yet been fully resolved. I think there is a very real case for both the federal government and the provincial governments to set up some kind of processing and marketing facilities for these crops in the initial stages. We know, for example, that into Alberta today thousands of carloads of fresh vegetables are imported, mostly from the United States, which could be grown right in southern Alberta. We know


there is more than one reason why this would be beneficial. For example, there is our international balance of payments which keeps cropping up as a problem. I suggest there are millions of dollars worth of these crops we could grow right at home if we only had the processing and distributing facilities available to us.
This is not an easy matter. It is difficult to get anyone to invest money in processing plants and distribution channels until there are a relatively large number of farmers in the area successfully growing the crops which it is intended should be produced on a larger scale. On the other hand, it is difficult to get farmers to begin to grow some of these crops and to gain experience unless there is a processing plant and a market available so that the work is profitable. I think the solution is to have producers co-operative enterprises underwritten by financing from both levels of government.
In addition, there is a very real need for a national sugar policy which would put some kind of stability into sugar prices both for the benefit of the consumer and the producer. We know that during the last two years or so sugar prices have been very high. In my opinion they have been too high. The sugar beet producers in my constituency agree that the price does not need to be as high as it is today. If they could be given some assurance that there would be a long term price guarantee in exchange for lowering the price a little now, they would be very happy to accept this.
I believe the government has been offered sugar on a long term basis at a price substantially less than Canada is paying today. All the government needs to do to take advantage of this is to commit Canada to buying the sugar over a period of seven or eight years into the future. This, in my view, would have a doubly beneficial effect. It would lead to an immediate reduction in the price of sugar to Canadian consumers and, second, it would provide that long term stability for which the beet producers have been asking for years. I hope that when we consider the better utilization and conservation of water we will also remember that these other problems of marketing and processing exist, and that it is the business of government not only to set up the capital works in the first instance but to follow through with some kind of assistance; and I suggest some kind of financial underwriting of these establishments would be the most useful, so as to see we make the optimum use of this water when it comes.
There is one other matter I wish to deal with and it relates to the subject of ARDA, which is dealt with both in the amendment

and in the subamendment. There is another vitally important water resource which has been barely touched in Canada, namely groundwater reserves. As hon. members who are interested in this subject know, the Alberta research council has been doing a great deal of work to find the extent of our groundwater reserves and has been successful in finding some aquifers. There is an important one running right into Medicine Hat and I am told there is an enormous one going across Montana into Saskatchewan-it is probably the old river bed of the Missouri river.
I do not know that this ground water reserve has been completely delineated and I suggest there is some important work which could be done in drilling of the area to find out where this reserve runs, to mark its edges and to determine its capacity. It is of particular importance this summer because in southern Alberta and southwestern Saskatchewan the traditional source of water from the spring run-off has been almost non-existent as far as surface water for stock watering is concerned. I think that under P.F.R.A., or under the auspices of any other government agency, such as ARDA, there is a very real need to do further work to locate the groundwater resources we have. It would make it much easier for farmers to drill wells if they had a reasonable assurance that they were likely to find water at certain levels.
I think it is a good idea for us to have taken part in such a debate as this. It seems to me there is general agreement in all political parties that some discussion on water resource management is needed. But I do not believe we can lay all the blame on the present government for the particular difficulties we are experiencing at the moment.

speakeroldname: Mr. John N. Turner (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I listened with interest this evening to the observations of the hon. member who has just resumed his seat, the hon. member for Medicine Hat (Mr. Olson) and also to the hon. member for Burnaby-Coquit-lam (Mr. Douglas) who, in analysing the water resource policy of this country, thought it well to say that the erosion of generations could not be laid at the door of a government which has been in office for just over 12 months, and that the responsibility for water management in Canada, although subject, quite properly, to review in this house from time to time, is not a matter upon which condemnation ought to be levelled against the present government.
I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that this amendment is phrased as an attempt to hold the present administration responsible for the work of generations. When one reads it, it
Canadian Water Resources becomes evident that it attempts to hold a government which has been in office for 12 months responsible for low water levels on the great lakes, although any student of the situation or any reasonable citizen of Canada will realize readily that this is a cyclical process dependant on factors altogether outside the scope of any particular administration in the short term.
What about dredging?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I would say that this afternoon the official opposition certainly had to dredge up a pretty weak argument-
Just dredge our harbours.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
-and muddy the waters, if I may say so, in an attempt to find some subject on which to criticize this administration. So far as water levels are concerned, and the cyclical trend, I will cite figures later to show that this has been a gradual process.
Let us look at the second subject, pollution. I might say that no steps of any consequence were taken by the previous administration with regard to pollution.
Oh, oh.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I see there is a lively reaction on the other side. The first concrete step that was taken was the reference earlier this spring, as the result of a debate held in this chamber on March 9, of the matter of pollution to the 10 provincial ministers of natural resources by the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources (Mr. Laing), so that the Canadian council of resource ministers could make a study of this problem.
I have mentioned the first two headings under which the government is being criticized, low water levels and increasing pollution, and the third heading is the conservation of water. At the outset I should like to draw to the attention of the house that the first legislation enacted in this country, involving the various provincial, municipal, regional and federal bodies having jurisdiction over the water resources of the country, was the Canada Water Conservation Act which was enacted on the 14th of May, 1953 under the former Liberal administration.
I cite this history, Mr. Speaker, because in listening to the amendment proposed by the hon. member for Brandon-Souris (Mr. Dinsdale) it was hard to divine just what he was criticizing the government for. He began by talking about what he called the long years of neglect, and we wondered for a moment whether we were being criticized in this amendment to a supply motion in May, 1964, for what had happened prior to 1957. It was quite coincidental, I am sure, that the
2910	HOUSE OF
Canadian Water Resources hon. member for Brandon-Souris, who after all should know the facts and should know better since he once held the national resources portfolio, did not cite any facts with which to back up his argument. Indeed, Mr. Speaker, the facts prior to 1957 do not bear the type of scrutiny that he avoided.
What were the facts? I have cited the Canada Water Conservation Act of 1953, the first conservation act passed by a federal parliament. Prior to 1957 there were agreements made with Ontario concerning the Shand dam, the Fanshaw dam and the Luther marsh dam.
For the Saskatchewan dam?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: My friend knows his geography better than that. One of my confreres suggests to me that in the circumstances perhaps I am being a little generous in making that remark. In any event, the policy initiated by the government prior to 1957 was continued by the previous Conservative administration, but only in 1961. It was four years before another agreement was signed. The upper Thames conservation authority agreement was signed in 1961 and the same year the metro Toronto and region conservation authority and the Parkhill dam project were initiated.
On a point of order, Mr. Speaker, the parliamentary secretary has either inadvertently or purposely left out the agreement in 1957 concerning the Napanee river conservation authority.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I have to advise the hon. member for Prince Ed-ward-Lennox that there is no point of order.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I was citing a particular piece of legislation, Mr. Speaker, and I doubt whether the learned member opposite could fit the particular project he has in mind into the particular piece of legislation I was citing.
On a point of order, the conservation authority signed an agreement with the Ontario department of development.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: Order.
It is the same category.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
speechtext: I should point out to the hon. member and to the house that if the hon. member disagrees with anything the hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George is now saying, he has the opportunity of refuting it when he rises to speak but his objection to anything the hon. member is saying now constitutes neither a point of privilege nor a point of order. The hon. member for St. Lawrence-St. George.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Thank you, Mr. Speaker. Subsequent to April 8, 1963, under legislation to which I have been referring we have under negotiation Fraser river diking at an estimated cost of close to $5 million. If I may turn to other legislation prior to 1957, the Red river basin investigation was started in 1950 and completed in 1953 at which time the federal government prepared, as the house well knows, comprehensive plans for flood control. I would also recall to the house the lakes Winnipeg and Manitoba board, the purpose of which was to study the resources of water flowing into and out of lakes Winnipeg and Manitoba. This study was initiated in 1956 and the reports were submitted in 1958.
Then there is the Fraser river board which was established in 1949, reconstituted in 1955 and directed to report its findings with respect to the effective regulation of that great river for flood control and power generation, and the resultant effects on fisheries, navigation, silting, erosion and irrigation. This is my answer to the hon. member for Brandon-Souris who said that in the matter of the control, management and conservation of water resources there had been long years of neglect.
Then he went on to say that he wished to criticize the present government for the slowing down of momentum. He referred to it as a tragic loss of momentum and said that there had been no new initiative in the area of renewable resources. Let us look for a moment at the momentum which existed, if it did, in the years 1957 to 1963.
Did it ever.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I hear the voice of that speedy Gonzales from the north. When he is not flying home he is flying by the seat of the pants in the house.
It is better than flying blind.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
What were the facts between 1957 and 1963? The hon. member for Brandon-Souris said he did not want to go into details, and I do not blame him at all. He mentioned the speech made by the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Diefenbaker) in Winnipeg in 1958. What happened after that speech? There were three silent years. Finally, in October, 1961 there was the resources for tomorrow conference, which was a considerable achievement. But where was that momentum?
What explains that three year vacuum between that great speech at Winnipeg and the conference that was finally held in 1961? If that is the record we are supposed to emulate I can say with some confidence now that we have no fear that record will be surpassed

under this administration. The previous administration, if this is moving with deliberate speed, waited until October 1961 before it finally established the Canadian council of resource ministers, and a plenary meeting was held in September of the next year. There was a four and a half year period that elapsed before the first plenary meeting of the resource ministers council which was forecast in Winnipeg, that central point in our confederation. If that is the type of speed we are being asked to emulate, again I think I can say on behalf of those on this side that we have no fear of being able to equal or surpass that type of record.
When this administration took over, there was just the shell of a program. The first meeting of any consequence was held last fall, on November 20 and 21. For the first time the ten provincial ministers of natural resources and the federal minister of resources met under the chairmanship of the minister from Quebec, the Hon. Rene Levesque-
Oh, oh.

-who, I might say, was a very able chairman indeed. For the first time some substance was given to this organization. As a result of these meetings all the present resource agreements between the provinces, and between the provinces and the federal government are being looked into by a permanent secretariat. The secretariat was set up by this administration, after four long years of waiting, following that great speech in Winnipeg. There was nothing but an idea, virtually nothing but a vision for four and a half years under the previous administration, and this project was finally put into action by this administration.
As I say, currently the renewable resource agreements between the provinces themselves, and the provinces and the federal government are being reviewed by this permanent secretariat which was set up by this government. There is being undertaken, under the jurisdiction of this national council of Canadian resource ministers, a review of the existing wildlife and fisheries agreements of this country. There is being undertaken an assessment of the ARDA program so that there can be a full discussion of the adequacy or otherwise of the ARDA projects at the next plenary meeting of the council this June in Prince Edward Island. Participation and planning of Canada's part in the international hydrologic decade was approved by this council last November. Preliminary work is now under way in connection with further important aspects of water conservation and water resources, among which I have already mentioned pollution. Now, this being so in
Canadian Water Resources so far as federal-provincial resource management of renewable resource development is concerned, this administration has nothing of which to be ashamed. On the contrary, within the last seven or eight months, the Canadian council of resource ministers has begun to function as a permanent body with a full time secretariat with projects which it can accomplish and which should be a credit to the country.
Let me say that I listened with great interest to the speech made by the hon. member for Brome-Missisquoi (Mr. Grafftey) whose efforts must have exhausted him. He spoke about co-operative federalism. He accused some of us of smiling. Perhaps there were some of us who were thinking of that great project of co-operative federalism in the area of water resources undertaken during the term of the administration which he was so bravely defending, the Columbia river treaty. He talked about the necessity for consultation between the federal and provincial governments. Here we have a treaty signed with great ceremony in November of 1961 and, lo and behold, someone came to the realization that the provincial jurisdiction over the resource, the entity whose water it was and the people who had the primary access and right to that water, had not given any agreement to what had been transacted by the federal government.
If this is an example of the co-operative federalism which the hon. member from Brome-Missisquoi had in mind, of course we had occasion to smile. Surely no greater example has been given to us in the history of the federal process as it deals with the resources of this country of a lack of proper consultation, of a lack of proper agreement, than the failure of the last administration to take the province of British Columbia into its confidence before signing an international treaty.
Without the protocol, Mr. Speaker, without the sales agreement, British Columbia would not have participated. It was through the efforts of this government and the negotiating team led by the minister of external affairs in this administration that what was once a hopeless morass, became something fulfilled, something truly co-operative.
The hon. member for Bumaby-Coquitlam said he was frightened by what the hon. member for Coast-Capilano (Mr. Davis) had said. He outlined an argument he has used before, as has his seatmate tonight, the hon. member for Kootenay West (Mr. Herridge).
Because they are unanswerable.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
Unanswerable?-they have been answered for five weeks in the committee on external affairs.

Canadian Water Resources
By whom?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
It is strange, you know, that a party that prides itself upon its imagination should really be so reactionary, so frightened, about dealing in Canada's natural resources and dealing with the future of this country. It is possible today to divert one watershed into another. Modern engineering has given scope to this country and utilization of its greatest natural resources for the benefit of all the people of Canada. Does he not realize, Mr. Speaker, that given the engineering feasibility, at any point in time, any kind of engineering solution can become economically practicable, and Canada has unlimited horizons, unlimited possibilities to develop its natural resources?
I am turning now, if I may-
When did you change your mind about the Columbia?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: I always had my mind made up about that particular treaty, when properly negotiated.
Like the hon. member for Kootenay East.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext: There was a parks policy mentioned this afternoon. Let me say to the house that for the first time, on November 18 to November 20, a federal parks conference met not merely at the technical level as had occurred under the previous administration, but at the technical and ministerial level, so that for the first time there was an opportunity to combine technical management and policy. I might say that as a result of that conference in November this country can now look forward to a review and a development of certain of the important aspects of our parklands. At that meeting there was discussed the assessment of non-urban park-lands, the factors relating to the selection of parklands, the relationship between provincial lands and national parks, park planning and design, and zoning as a step in the over-all planning of large parks. Finally, in co-operation with the ten provincial jurisdictions and the federal government, we have a co-ordinated parks policy.
What about the territories?

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Northern Affairs and National Resources
speechtext:
I would not, of course, overlook the territories and I think the learned member for Yukon (Mr. Nielsen) will quite realize that, but for the moment I think the general term federal be wide enough to encompass the lands he has described.
Nothing could be more important to this country than water. The hon. member for Parry Sound-Muskoka (Mr. Aiken) was citing water levels to the house and was trying to relate them in terms of a recent change


in climatic and geographical conditions to the responsibilities of the government. I want to read into the record the water levels for lake Huron during the last four years, all taken during the month of March. The long term average level over the period from 1860 to 1963 was 578.36 feet above sea level. In March 1961 the level of lake Huron, below that average level, was 0.53 feet; in March 1962 it was 1.02 feet; in 1963 it was 2.11 feet and in March of this year it was 2.97 feet.
I am citing these figures to illustrate that this trend or cycle in water levels had begun as early as March 1961, and was part of a long term cycle that has been prevalent in Canada over the years. Let me now deal with the annual outflows from lake Huron. The long term average over the same years was 189,000 cubic feet per second, or 11.6 inches of the drainage basin. In 1961 the annual outflow was 182,000 cubic feet per second; in 1962 it was 177,000 cubic feet per second and in 1963 it was 163,000 cubic feet per second, so that the trend as long ago as three or four years, was the same trend that we are experiencing today.
I now wish to emphasize to the house that the outflow from lake Huron has decreased in relation to the increase in water levels. To make the figures clear, I have to set out the annual inflows into lakes Michigan and Huron, where the long term average has been 189,000 cubic feet per second. In 1961 the inflow was 165,000 cubic feet per second; in 1962 it was 149,000 cubic feet per second, and in 1963 it was 153,000 cubic feet per second, so that the inflow below normal of a small amount has a large effect on the lake levels,' because the level also of the drainage basin, was lowered from the long term average of 11.6 inches to 10.6 inches in 1961, 9.1 inches in 1962 and 9.4 inches in 1963. Here again the trend has not been a sudden one. The trend was something that was foreseeable, something which has been a gradual process.
This government is conscious of the value of water, and tomorrow we hope to illustrate to the house what its policy is with respect to its management as a resource. It is not merely a question of level; it is a question of the interaction of all the interrelated resources. It has to do with the runoff from timber lands, the run-off from cultivated rural areas, the increased consumption of water, and precipitation. It has to do with a number of interrelated factors which are all brought together to an end result, so that any water policy must take into account not only the present yield and profit of water but also the inventory and the deferred benefits.

We will suggest to the house that in a well managed watershed we need an interrelation of forest policy, of agrarian farm policy, of preventives against erosion, against the waste of soil, control of industrial use and of sewage in order to control pollution, together with a fire prevention policy.
Now, Mr. Speaker, before I yield the floor to the hour this evening may I say that I feel the official opposition in presenting this motion and in trying to attribute water levels, that have been developing in cycles, to the actions of this administration is merely indulging in a partisan manoeuvre. The management of our water resources is something in which we are all vitally interested as Canadians, and the official opposition is trying to convert this problem into a trumped up motion of want of confidence.
May I call it ten o'clock, Mr. Speaker?

We in the maritimes, and this is not confined to New Brunswick alone, have been much interested in the prospect of the great potential development of the Passamaquoddy power project. We feel that this might be an important and major device which would assist us to help ourselves economically, along with those other great projects which I could list in order of priority as the causeway, the corridor road and the Chignecto development.
This Passamaquoddy development should concern all of us in this national parliament. I have been wondering in recent months whether the government of the nation is in fact as concerned as it should be about this important matter. I have read what Premier Robichaud has said; I have read what the leader of the opposition, Mr. Sherwood, has said; and we all know, thanks to his brilliant head and fine mind, what Brigadier Wardell thinks. We know how he has galvanized the interest of the maritime provinces in this matter as well as in other laudable projects. We in the maritimes, who have lost so many brains, have finally received one from another area. Brigadier Wardell is in the foremost category of such persons and he has become a tribune of the maritimes.
We are interested, too, in the tremendous concern which the United States, at the congressional level and at the state level has in this project. The executive level and the state of Maine have shown they are tremendously interested. Their government has moved motions to have something done about the Passamaquoddy. We ask, what is the government of Canada doing; what is it thinking? I looked and listened the other day when the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Martin) reported on the Canada-United States meeting. The Secretary of State for External Affairs, with all his many virtues, is not one given to laconic brevity, but out of his fulsome report we found only this: "We heard from the United States their ideas on the possible development of Passamaquoddy tidal power." I ask, Mr. Speaker, for some of the ideas of the present government on this hopeful, important, tremendous potential development of the Passamaquoddy.
Is the dominion government interested? What steps will it take, other than listening to the suggestions of the United States, which is apparently prepared to extend tremendous amounts of money to provide for us power at cheaper rates than we have ever had

subtopic: BENEFITS TO CANADIAN WORKERS IN STATE OF MAINE
BENEFITS TO CANADIAN WORKERS IN STATE OF MAINE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the point I wish to deal with tonight has been raised on several instances in the house. It has to do with the unemployment insurance of Canadian lumbermen who go to work in the state of Maine.
Indeed, the question has been brought up here for more than ten years, and very seldom has a minister of labour been able to give a satisfactory reply.
The delay in solving this problem is rather hard to understand, considering that the two governments involved get along so well together when it comes to signing an agreement on nuclear arms or sending troops to a foreign land. This goodwill between them should not keep them in the clouds; they should come down to earth and realize that the thousands of people who live near the Canada-United States border wish to see their problems solved satisfactorily as soon as possible.
Agreements have been signed between Canada and 46 American states so that Canadians and Americans who go and work across the border are still entitled to unemployment insurance benefits. Only four states, namely Maine, New Hampshire and two others, have not yet come to terms with Canada in that respect.
Mr. Speaker, I am not aware of the reasons why such an agreement cannot be reached with the state of Maine in favour of the lumbermen who go over there to work.
I would like the Minister of Labour (Mr. MacEachen) to tell us, on behalf of the government, the reasons why an agreement cannot be reached with the state of Maine concerning Canadian lumbermen.
In my opinion, Mr. Speaker, a simple exchange of correspondence between that state and the Canadian government is not good enough to settle that ticklish problem and, futhermore, I do not know whether serious meetings have been held between officials of that state and the Canadian government. I would like to obtain information in respect of meetings which may have been held between the authorities concerned, and if no negotiations have been undertaken I would ask the Minister of Labour to negotiate an agreement with the state of Maine on behalf of the Canadian government.
I hope the Minister of Labour will permit me to offer him a solution to that serious problem. Could he not include in the Unemployment Insurance Act a provision whereby any lumberman going into a neighbouring

state, especially Maine, to work at his trade would be eligible to receive unemployment insurance benefits upon his return.
In my opinion the lack of an agreement to this effect between the state of Maine and the Canadian government constitutes a burden for the latter, since a growing number of bush workers have stopped going to the United States because they find that, when they come back to Canada after working over there five or six months, they are unable to get unemployment insurance benefits. We find such cases especially in my riding and in the neighbouring constituencies of Beauce, Lot-biniere and Bellechasse, where more and more bush workers are unemployed.
The minister is a very hard worker who wants to reduce unemployment and help the jobless in Canada.
Therefore, I wish he would tell me what obstacles stand in the way of such an agreement between the Canadian government and the state of Maine in particular.

speakeroldname: Hon. A. J. MacEachen (Minister of Labour):
subtopic: BENEFITS TO CANADIAN WORKERS IN STATE OF MAINE
speechtext:
In the short moments at my disposal I should try to give the hon. member the information he desires in this connection. There is no lack of desire on the part of the Canadian government or of the unemployment insurance commission to enter into a reciprocal arrangement with the state of Maine. Negotiations between the commission and the state of Maine on this problem have continued for a period of 18 years, and shortly after I became the Minister of Labour I discovered that in all those years the state of Maine had said neither no nor yes to the proposals which had been made by successive Canadian governments.
I undertook last September to go down to the capital of Maine where I met with the governor and the head of the employment security commission, and put forward as forcibly as I could the strong reasons why Maine ought to agree to an arrangement of this sort between herself and Canada. The assurance I received was that Maine would give a definite answer. Five or six weeks later the chief commissioner received a letter stating that Maine would not enter into this kind of reciprocal arrangement.
The hon. member will understand the reasons for this refusal; they are understandable if not commendable. Because of the experience-rating system operative in the state of Maine under the employment security arrangements, the less employment prevailing in any industry the smaller the rate of contribution by the employer, who is the exclusive contributor to the unemployment in-20220-185
