Knowing that the Minister of National Health and Welfare is in hospital I should like to wish her a speedy recovery. I hope she overcomes her difficulties as quickly as possible.
The royal commission on government organization, commonly known as the Glassco commission, made the following recommendation in one of its reports, with respect to Indian health services. I should like to quote from page 201 of the third volume of the report which advises-
-that a positive program be developed for the more rapid transfer of Indian health care to normal community facilities in populated areas of the provinces.
Because of this and because of the government's decision with respect to veterans hospitals I raised this matter by way of a question to the minister on the 30th of March and I got the answer that there was to be no change, and that there would have been an announcement if there was going to be a change. Subsequently I received a copy of the local newspaper, the Prince Rupert News. It contained an article quoting the speaker of the provincial legislature and a reference by him to the minister of health of British Columbia. The effect of the article was that the Miller Bay hospital, which comes under the jurisdiction of the federal department, was to be closed.
Based upon that report I asked another question. Finally, on the 13th of April I received a lengthy, detailed answer read by the parliamentary secretary to the effect that the Miller Bay hospital would be closed at some time in the future as a hospital for the treatment of tubercular cases and as a hospital for general care purposes, but that no time limit had been established. I posed a supplementary question and got an answer by way of a letter which I think should be put on the record because it should have been put on Hansard in the first place. The letter is dated April 16, 1964. It is from the Minister of National Health and Welfare (Miss La-Marsh), and the relevant part reads as follows:
Any special grant made on behalf of the Indian population would have to be the subject of a

Proceedings on Adjournment Motion request from the Prince Rupert general hospital and would be dealt with on its merits when costs involved were presented to the department.
Because of the implications of that letter I think it should be on Hansard so that the general public, and particularly the people involved in Prince Rupert, will be able to see it. There are reports circulating in Prince Rupert and in the Miller Bay hospital at the present time, which reached their peak a day or two ago, to the effect that the Miller Bay hospital is to be reduced from its present 187 bed capacity to only 14 beds by the end of 1965, and there are also rumours that it will be closing shortly thereafter. But nowhere has there been any official declaration that this is not to be the case. Consequently there is great concern.
This is a very serious matter, Mr. Speaker, because the hospital is the only one of its sort in northern British Columbia. Between five and ten thousand native Indian people are involved, and in my opinion the government should make a statement of policy about its intentions not only with respect to the Miller Bay hospital specifically but with respect to all the hospitals which come under the Department of Northern Affairs and National Resources. We would welcome such a statement so that everybody will know where they stand. I would ask the government to keep in mind that the minister herself had no difficulty in getting into a hospital, but if the Miller Bay hospital happens to close many native Indian people in northern British Columbia who may want to get into a hospital will not be able to because the facilities will not be there.

speakeroldname: Mr. J. C. Munro (Parliamentary Secretary to Minister of National Health and Welfare):
speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of National Health and Welfare
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would point out to the hon. hon. member for Skeena (Mr. Howard) that in the answer to his question given on April 13 last it was pointed out that this hospital was originally to service tubercular Indians, and the case load of tubercular Indians has been reduced to such an extent that the hospital has been gradually converted to a general hospital. In the answer it was also pointed out that the hospital was not going to be phased out, so far as use by the Indians in the area is concerned, until such time as the Prince Rupert general hospital had adequate beds available for the Indians. The reason given for even contemplating the phasing out of the hospital at Miller Bay was that it was of old wartime construction, was not an adequate facility, nor by implication safe.
I am sure that the department is concerned, as a result of the hon. member's representation, that the Indians have proper medical care. However, I do not see anything in the answer which is indicative of the policy of the department which should unduly disturb either the hon. member or the Indian, because it is clearly stated there is no intention of closing out the hospital. I do not believe we should be too concerned about rumours the hon. member may have heard, since there is no intention of closing out the hospital until adequate facilities at the Prince Rupert general hospital are available to take care of the Indian.
